papers.paper_title: ORGANIC REACTION MECHANISMS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think organic reactions can be understood simply by assuming that the most nearby groups on a two-dimensional drawing react with each other directly, with the hydrogen of one hydroxyl and the whole hydroxyl group of the other combining to form water.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Mechanisms must be explained by electron movement and actual bond-making/bond-breaking, not by merely connecting nearby groups on a drawing.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify nucleophiles, electrophiles, and electron-pair movements, then show which bonds break and form in a sequence that is chemically and stereochemically plausible rather than relying on proximity in the formula drawing.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the most proximate groups react with each other"
misconceptions.source_title: ORGANIC REACTION MECHANISMS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may fail to see how an epoxide ring is formed if they reason only from the starting structures without tracking the stepwise electron movement.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The epoxide forms through stepwise acid/base deprotonation, nucleophilic attack, then intramolecular ring closure with bromide leaving.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should follow each intermediate: base removes the acidic proton, the resulting anion attacks the carbonyl, and the alkoxide then attacks the carbon bearing bromine to close the three-membered ring and expel bromide.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it is not immediately obvious how the epoxide ring has been formed"
misconceptions.source_title: ORGANIC REACTION MECHANISMS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may predict the product stereochemistry by a direct substitution/lasso-style argument and conclude that (2S,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane should be the product.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The reaction proceeds through a bridged bromonium ion, leading to racemization at the relevant center and formation of a racemic mixture.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the predicted stereochemical outcome with experiment and infer that a bridged intermediate is required because it explains backside opening from either end and the observed racemic product.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "this analysis would predict that when (2S,3S)-3-bromobutan-2-ol reacts with HBr, the stereochemistry of the resultant product would be (2S,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane"
misconceptions.source_title: ORGANIC REACTION MECHANISMS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may assume that if a mechanism predicts a single stereoisomer, the product will be optically active, and may overlook the possibility of a racemic mixture with no optical activity.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A reaction can yield an equal mixture of enantiomers, which is optically inactive overall.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should consider whether a reaction creates enantiomers in equal amounts; if both are formed equally, the product mixture is racemic and has no net optical rotation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the product is a mixture, which comprises an equal amount of (2S,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane and (2R,3R)-2,3-dibromobutane, and which displays no optical activity"
misconceptions.source_title: ORGANIC REACTION MECHANISMS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not understand that curved arrows represent electron-pair movement and therefore may miss the actual sequence of bond changes in a mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Curved arrows indicate the movement of electron pairs between molecular orbitals and allow one to track bond making and bond breaking.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret each curved arrow as the movement of two electrons from a donor orbital/lone pair or bond to an acceptor site, then update formal charges and connectivity step by step.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The movement of the electron pairs is indicated by the use of a curved arrow"
misconceptions.source_title: ORGANIC REACTION MECHANISMS

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may overlook that carbon cannot exceed four covalent bonds during a substitution or ring-closing step.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Carbon should not be shown with more than four covalent bonds at any instant in a valid mechanism.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should ensure that as one bond forms, another bond breaks if necessary, so carbon’s valence is never exceeded during intermediate steps.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the carbon never has more than four covalent bonds around its nucleus at any one time"
misconceptions.source_title: ORGANIC REACTION MECHANISMS

papers.paper_title: Analysis of undergraduate chemistry students' responses to substitution reaction mechanisms: a road to mastery

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat SN2 reactions as if they proceed by an SN1 pathway with a carbocation intermediate.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN2 reactions occur in a single concerted step with no carbocation intermediate.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that SN2 involves backside attack by the nucleophile and simultaneous leaving-group departure, so there is no discrete carbocation stage to draw or describe.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Most students ignored the carbocation intermediates provided in the questions for the SN1 reaction mechanism and drew SN2 mechanisms for these questions."
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed as a common error; the paper reports that students' correct SN2 arrow responses were 17.1% and 14.3%, while SN1 correct arrow responses were only 1.4% and 2.9%.
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of undergraduate chemistry students' responses to substitution reaction mechanisms: a road to mastery

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe SN2 mechanisms include carbocation formation and nucleophilic attack on that carbocation.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN2 mechanisms do not form a carbocation; the nucleophile attacks as the leaving group departs in one step.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain SN2 as a concerted substitution where the nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon while the leaving group leaves, all in the same step, without any carbocation intermediate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Again, SN2 reaction mechanisms do not proceed with the formation of a carbocation intermediate, but students were talking about the formation of carbocations and nucleophilic attack of carbocations in their explanations of SN2 reaction mechanisms."
misconceptions.prevalence: Described as a pattern in the incorrect explanations; incorrect explanation rates for SN2 explanation items were 45.7% and 57.1%.
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of undergraduate chemistry students' responses to substitution reaction mechanisms: a road to mastery

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that leaving-group departure means elimination and nucleophilic attack means substitution, treating the two as separate events in the same reaction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In substitution reactions, the nucleophile replaces the leaving group; elimination is a different reaction pathway involving loss of groups to form unsaturation.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish reaction types by the overall outcome and electron flow: substitution replaces one group with another, whereas elimination forms a new pi bond by removing atoms/groups.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This elimination and substitution reaction occurs simultaneously. As the bromine atom is cleaved away, a nucleophile attaches to the carbocation formed at the same time"
misconceptions.prevalence: Reported as a common feature of incorrect responses; no exact count provided.
misconceptions.population: Subset of students who provided incorrect explanations
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of undergraduate chemistry students' responses to substitution reaction mechanisms: a road to mastery

misconceptions.subtopic: SN1 vs SN2 mechanism identification in explanations
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students use the wrong named mechanism, for example calling an SN2 reaction an E1 or SN1 process, based on surface cues.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should identify the mechanism from the actual reaction pathway and electron movement, not from isolated cues like leaving-group quality.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should match the described reactants, products, intermediates, and electron-pushing pattern to the correct mechanism name before explaining it.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Akosua's explanation was as follows: 'The mechanism undergoes E1 substitution. The bromine atom is a better leaving group'."
misconceptions.prevalence: Presented as an example of the incorrect explanation category; incorrect explanations were 45.7% to 65.7% across items.
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of undergraduate chemistry students' responses to substitution reaction mechanisms: a road to mastery

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students interpret the first SN1 step as if the leaving-group departure itself is the whole reaction and stop there.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN1 is a two-step process: leaving-group departure to form a carbocation, followed by nucleophilic attack, and often a deprotonation step if needed.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should describe both the formation of the carbocation intermediate and the subsequent nucleophilic attack, showing the full multistep pathway.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "a lot of students described only the first part of the given SN1 reaction mechanisms (the leaving of the leaving group leading to the formation of a carbocation intermediate)"
misconceptions.prevalence: A significant number of students gave only partial explanations; partial explanations ranged from 10% to 21.4%.
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of undergraduate chemistry students' responses to substitution reaction mechanisms: a road to mastery

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students draw curved arrows without assigning correct electron-flow meaning to them and may use arrows from the wrong direction or omit required arrows.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Curved arrows must represent electron movement from an electron-rich source to an electron-poor site, with all necessary steps shown.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should trace electrons from a lone pair, bond, or negative charge to the electrophilic site and include each step of the mechanism without reverse or missing arrows.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students did not attribute meaning to the electron-pushing arrows and did not consider whether the mechanisms they had drawn were chemically reasonable or not"
misconceptions.prevalence: Common across arrow-type responses; correct mechanism rates ranged from 1.4% to 17.1%, while incorrect mechanism rates ranged from 71.4% to 78.6%.
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of undergraduate chemistry students' responses to substitution reaction mechanisms: a road to mastery

papers.paper_title: Inadequacies of the S<sub>N</sub>1 Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe solvolysis proceeds by a two-step SN1 mechanism in which a planar free carbocation forms first and then the solvent attacks from either side.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In these solvolysis reactions, a free solvated carbocation intermediate is not required; the paper argues for a bimolecular one-step process with inversion in each elementary substitution step and reversibility overall.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use stereochemical and isotopic evidence to reason that if every substitution step occurs with inversion and exchange/racemization and isotope incorporation occur together, a reversible substitution pathway can explain the observations without invoking a long-lived free carbocation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the slow formation of a planar carbocation intermediate, followed by fast addition of solvent from either of the two sides"
misconceptions.population: Textbook-authored student/teaching context; the paper reports "many" students later accepted textbook views
misconceptions.source_title: Inadequacies of the S<sub>N</sub>1 Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe complete racemization in SN1 solvolysis is explained by a carbocation being attacked equally from both sides.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The paper argues that racemization can arise from reversible substitution steps with inversion in each direction, not necessarily from a free carbocation attacked equally from both faces.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish overall racemization from the mechanism of a single step and recognize that forward and reverse inversions can generate racemate even when each substitution step is stereospecific.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Still, this leaves unexplained why there is racemization and why it is not complete."
misconceptions.source_title: Inadequacies of the S<sub>N</sub>1 Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe SN1 means first the leaving group departs and then the nucleophile attacks, with SN2 being the only simultaneous process.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The paper argues that both classes can be understood as one-step bond-making/bond-breaking processes with similar trigonal-bipyramidal transition states; the distinction is better framed by reversibility, reagents, and stereochemical outcome than by an oversimplified step order.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from transition-state geometry and stereochemical inversion that bond breaking and bond forming are coupled in the elementary step rather than occurring as isolated sequential events.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The difference between the SN1 and SN2 mechanisms is in the timing of the steps. In the SN1 mechanism, first X leaves, then Y attacks. In the SN2 case, the two things happen simultaneously."
misconceptions.population: Textbook learners; the author reports many students accepted this textbook summary
misconceptions.source_title: Inadequacies of the S<sub>N</sub>1 Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students expect stereoisomeric substrates that form the same free carbocation to give identical solvolytic products.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The paper argues that different stereoisomeric substrates can give different products because the reaction does not proceed through a common free carbocation; stereochemistry of the reacting molecule influences the pathway.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should predict that if stereochemistry is retained in the reacting system and each step requires a specific anti arrangement, then different isomers can follow different trajectories and produce different products.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Such pairs should give identical free carbocations, hence identical solvolytic products, but they give instead dramatically different products"
misconceptions.source_title: Inadequacies of the S<sub>N</sub>1 Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume isotope incorporation under solvolytic conditions only supports an SN1 carbocation mechanism and not a substitution process with inversion.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The paper presents isotope-exchange experiments as evidence that degenerate substitution can occur with inversion, consistent with a reversible bimolecular process.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect equal rates of racemization and isotope incorporation to repeated substitution events, each proceeding with inversion, rather than to long-lived carbocations.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "each step should occur with inversion, and if the three R groups are different... the rate of isotope incorporation and the rate of racemization should be the same."
misconceptions.source_title: Inadequacies of the S<sub>N</sub>1 Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think alkyl carbocations are common reactive intermediates in nucleophilic solvolysis in water or alcohol.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The paper argues that alkyl carbocations are extremely reactive and generally do not persist in nucleophilic solvents; observed solvolysis need not involve free carbocations.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the high reactivity of carbocations and the nucleophilicity of the solvent to infer that a long-lived free cation is unlikely in water or alcohol.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "alkyl cations are extremely reactive and can only exist in the vacuum of a mass spectrometer or in non nucleophilic solvents"
misconceptions.population: Students in organic chemistry courses; the author states he warned students against believing in free carbocation intermediates
misconceptions.source_title: Inadequacies of the S<sub>N</sub>1 Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe the tertiary-to-primary reactivity trend in solvolysis is best explained by electronic stabilization of a carbocation intermediate.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The paper argues that the opposite reactivity trends under SN2 and solvolysis can be explained by steric effects, bond loosening, reversibility, and nucleofuge behavior without needing carbocation stabilization as the central explanation.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare how steric hindrance slows direct attack in SN2 and how favorable leaving-group behavior and bond loosening can make tertiary substrates react faster in solvolysis.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "One argument for the SN1 mechanism in solvolysis has been that a reactivity sequence ... is observed that runs parallel with the electronic stabilization of cations"
misconceptions.source_title: Inadequacies of the S<sub>N</sub>1 Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think that adding tight ion pairs, solvated ion pairs, solvent-separated ion pairs, simultaneous SN1/SN2, and borderline cases resolves the mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The paper argues these ad hoc categories do not solve the underlying problem of explaining solvolysis without unnecessary carbocation intermediates; a unified reversible bimolecular model is preferred.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate whether added intermediates improve explanatory power or merely complicate the mechanism, and prefer a model that accounts for stereochemistry, kinetics, and isotopic exchange consistently.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Winstein introduced a modification of Ingold's mechanism based on tight ion pairs, solvated ion pairs, and solvent-separated ion pairs"
misconceptions.source_title: Inadequacies of the S<sub>N</sub>1 Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may believe that if a solvolytic reaction is reversible, reversibility alone explains racemization.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The paper states that reversibility by itself does not explain racemization; one must consider that both forward and backward steps can invert configuration and thus partially cancel or produce net racemization depending on pathways.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should analyze the stereochemical consequence of both forward and reverse substitutions rather than assuming that equilibrium automatically gives racemate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "However, this reversibility alone does not explain the observed racemization, since inversion in the forward reaction is compensated by inversion in the backward reaction"
misconceptions.source_title: Inadequacies of the S<sub>N</sub>1 Mechanism

papers.paper_title: Absence of S<sub>N</sub>1 Involvement in the Solvolysis of Secondary Alkyl Compounds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Secondary alkyl compounds can undergo solvolysis with significant S_N1 involvement, or as 'borderline' cases between S_N1 and S_N2.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For the secondary alkyl substrates discussed in the paper, solvolysis proceeds only via S_N2 under the documented conditions; there is no support here for significant S_N1 involvement or borderline behavior.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the stereochemical evidence and the later kinetic/competition studies: when products show inversion rather than racemization, the mechanism is backside attack (S_N2). If all substitution products from secondary substrates are inverted under the studied conditions, then the reaction is not proceeding through a carbenium-ion S_N1 pathway.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "secondary alkyl compounds go only via the S_N2 mechanism"
misconceptions.population: Students using introductory organic chemistry texts and mechanistic interpretations of secondary-substrate solvolysis
misconceptions.source_title: Absence of S<sub>N</sub>1 Involvement in the Solvolysis of Secondary Alkyl Compounds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Secondary substrates in solvolysis form carbenium-ion intermediates that then give the substitution product.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For the secondary systems reviewed in the paper, the evidence supports direct substitution by S_N2 pathways rather than carbenium-ion intermediates.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect complete or near-complete inversion with direct backside attack and recognize that a carbocation intermediate would be expected to lead to racemization or loss of stereochemical information. Thus retained or inverted stereochemistry rules out a carbenium-ion mechanism for these cases.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "There is no support in the Ingold textbook (3) or in the literature for secondary systems exhibiting 'borderline' behavior or carbenium ion-type intermediates"
misconceptions.source_title: Absence of S<sub>N</sub>1 Involvement in the Solvolysis of Secondary Alkyl Compounds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Solvolysis of secondary alkyl compounds should give racemization because it is diagnostic of an S_N1 mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The documented secondary-substrate examples here give inversion, often essentially complete inversion, consistent with S_N2; racemization is not the expected outcome for these secondary systems under the conditions discussed.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from stereochemistry: S_N2 gives inversion by backside attack, while S_N1 through a planar carbocation tends toward racemization. Therefore an inverted alcohol product indicates S_N2 participation rather than S_N1.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the solvent reactions of sec-octyl bromide exhibit in considerable amount the racemization which is diagnostic of the unimolecular mechanism"
misconceptions.population: Students learning mechanistic stereochemistry from examples of sec-octyl bromide and related substrates
misconceptions.source_title: Absence of S<sub>N</sub>1 Involvement in the Solvolysis of Secondary Alkyl Compounds

misconceptions.target_misconception: A partially optically active product from secondary-substrate solvolysis is evidence for a mixed S_N1/S_N2 mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The paper argues that apparent intermediate optical purity can arise from competing stereospecific displacement pathways, not from S_N1 involvement. In the cited studies, even when optical purity is less than 100%, the underlying pathways can still be S_N2.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish product optical purity from mechanism. Intermediate ee can result from two S_N2 pathways with different stereochemical outcomes or from racemization before/after substitution, so ee alone does not prove S_N1. Mechanistic assignment requires considering the whole reaction network and stereochemical pathway.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Apparent racemization in mixed solvents is but the result of competitive but stereospecific displacement processes."
misconceptions.population: Students interpreting optical purity data in substitution reactions
misconceptions.source_title: Absence of S<sub>N</sub>1 Involvement in the Solvolysis of Secondary Alkyl Compounds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Mixed-solvent solvolysis of secondary sulfonates must proceed via S_N1 if racemization or apparent racemization is observed.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For the secondary sulfonates discussed, the observed behavior is explained by consecutive S_N2 displacement steps and competing pathways, not by an S_N1 carbocation mechanism.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should analyze the sequence of substitution steps: if one solvent molecule displaces the leaving group by S_N2 and then another nucleophile displaces the first, the net optical purity can change without any S_N1 step. Thus racemization-like results do not automatically imply carbocation formation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "all of the reactions went via S_N2 mechanisms with 100% inversion, but the alcohol was of intermediate optical purity because it was formed by two different pathways"
misconceptions.population: Students studying mixed-solvent solvolysis examples such as 2-octyl brosylate
misconceptions.source_title: Absence of S<sub>N</sub>1 Involvement in the Solvolysis of Secondary Alkyl Compounds

misconceptions.topic: Nucleophilic substitution trends across substrate classes
misconceptions.subtopic: primary and tertiary substrate mechanism percentages in the Ingold diagram
misconceptions.target_misconception: Primary substrates undergo about 20% S_N1 and tertiary substrates about 15% S_N2 in the general case.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The paper rejects these percentages as unsupported; under the simplified scheme presented, primary substrates go only via S_N2 and tertiary substrates go only via S_N1 under ionizing conditions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should not treat a textbook diagram as a universal rule when the paper explicitly states that later evidence does not support those partial percentages. Mechanistic assignment should follow substrate class and conditions: primary and methyl substrates are S_N2-only, tertiary substrates are S_N1-only under the relevant ionizing conditions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "There is no support ... for tertiary systems going ≈15% by an S_N2 mechanism; or for primary systems going ≈20% via an S_N1 mechanism."
misconceptions.population: Students relying on the Ingold textbook diagram for substitution mechanisms
misconceptions.source_title: Absence of S<sub>N</sub>1 Involvement in the Solvolysis of Secondary Alkyl Compounds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Any kinetically first-order substitution reaction must be S_N1, and first-order order alone proves a unimolecular mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Kinetic order alone does not prove mechanism; first-order behavior can arise from reaction conditions or mixed processes, and mechanism must be established by additional evidence such as stereochemistry and reaction pathway analysis.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should separate rate law from molecular mechanism. First-order kinetics may describe the rate-determining step, but one must still test whether the structure, stereochemistry, and competition experiments support a carbocation intermediate or some other pathway.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "they equate the kinetic order of a reaction with the molecularity of the reaction transition state"
misconceptions.population: Students who infer mechanism directly from rate-law order
misconceptions.source_title: Absence of S<sub>N</sub>1 Involvement in the Solvolysis of Secondary Alkyl Compounds

misconceptions.target_misconception: Secondary substrate solvolysis occurs without any nucleophilic participation only when an S_N1 carbocation intermediate is formed.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The paper concludes that secondary substrates can show substantial nucleophilic participation and still proceed by S_N2, including solvent-assisted S_N2 or competing S_N2 pathways.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that solvent participation does not automatically mean S_N1. If the transition state involves backside attack and inversion, nucleophilic participation is part of an S_N2 process, not evidence for a carbocation intermediate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This interpretation suggests a variation in the magnitude of nucleophilic solvent assistance in S_N2 transition states"
misconceptions.population: Students interpreting solvent-assisted substitution in secondary systems
misconceptions.source_title: Absence of S<sub>N</sub>1 Involvement in the Solvolysis of Secondary Alkyl Compounds

papers.paper_title: Challenges Faced by Teachers and Students in Teaching-Learning Reaction Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe reaction mechanisms are generally easy to understand, but the paper documents that many actually struggle to understand and write them.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A reaction mechanism should be understood as a stepwise explanation of how bonds break and form and how intermediates and arrows represent electron movement.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect each step of the mechanism to bond changes, electron movement, intermediates, and the overall transformation, rather than memorizing isolated steps.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I feel difficulty understanding the reaction mechanism."
misconceptions.prevalence: 62.5% strongly agreed; 7.5% agreed (70% total)
misconceptions.source_title: Challenges Faced by Teachers and Students in Teaching-Learning Reaction Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can easily write reaction mechanisms taught in class.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should be able to represent the mechanism step-by-step using correct arrows, intermediates, and bond changes.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: To write a mechanism, a student must identify the reacting species, follow electron flow with curly arrows, and show each transformation in the correct sequence.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I find it challenging to write reaction mechanisms taught in class."
misconceptions.prevalence: 37.5% strongly agreed; 10% agreed (47.5% total)
misconceptions.source_title: Challenges Faced by Teachers and Students in Teaching-Learning Reaction Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think SN1 and SN2 reaction mechanisms are straightforward or easy to learn.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN1 and SN2 mechanisms must be distinguished by their different rate laws, steps, intermediates, and substitution pathways.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare substrate, nucleophile, leaving group, solvent, and the presence or absence of a carbocation intermediate to determine the correct mechanism.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The concept of SN1 and SN2 reaction mechanisms is difficult for me."
misconceptions.prevalence: 50% strongly agreed; 25% disagreed (75% total reporting difficulty)
misconceptions.source_title: Challenges Faced by Teachers and Students in Teaching-Learning Reaction Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not recognize inductive, mesomeric, and electrometric effects as important factors in reaction mechanisms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: These electronic effects influence electron distribution, reactivity, and reaction pathways in organic mechanisms.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should link substituent effects and electron movement to reactivity and mechanistic outcome, using resonance and inductive reasoning where appropriate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The factors that affect the reaction rate, like inductive, mesomeric, and electrometric effects of the reaction mechanism, are challenging to learn."
misconceptions.prevalence: Reported qualitatively; no percentage given
misconceptions.source_title: Challenges Faced by Teachers and Students in Teaching-Learning Reaction Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students confuse the condition of bond fission and do not distinguish how bonds break in mechanisms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should distinguish homolytic from heterolytic bond fission and relate each to the products formed.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A correct explanation requires identifying whether electrons split equally or unequally during bond breaking and predicting the resulting radicals or ions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The condition of bond fission ... confuses me"
misconceptions.prevalence: Reported qualitatively; no percentage given
misconceptions.source_title: Challenges Faced by Teachers and Students in Teaching-Learning Reaction Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot identify the attacking reagents in a mechanism and are unsure which species is the electrophile or nucleophile.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should identify the electron-pair donor as the nucleophile and the electron-pair acceptor as the electrophile.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: By examining electron density and charge, a student should determine which species donates electrons and which species accepts them at each step.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the formation of attacking reagents identification confuses me"
misconceptions.prevalence: Reported qualitatively; no percentage given
misconceptions.source_title: Challenges Faced by Teachers and Students in Teaching-Learning Reaction Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot define or identify electrophiles and nucleophiles before studying the reaction mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrophiles are electron-pair acceptors and nucleophiles are electron-pair donors; identifying them is foundational for mechanism analysis.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use electron density, charge, and lone pairs to decide which species will attack and which will be attacked.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students are confused in identifying electrophiles and nucleophiles before studying reaction mechanism."
misconceptions.prevalence: 75% strongly agreed; 25% disagreed (teacher responses indicating student difficulty)
misconceptions.source_title: Challenges Faced by Teachers and Students in Teaching-Learning Reaction Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can easily define reaction intermediates.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reaction intermediates are transient species formed during a multi-step mechanism and must be distinguished from reactants and products.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify intermediates as species that appear in one step and are consumed in a later step, rather than final products or starting materials.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students themselves can define reaction intermediates easily"
misconceptions.prevalence: 25% strongly agreed; 50% agreed; 25% disagreed (teachers' responses show divided views)
misconceptions.source_title: Challenges Faced by Teachers and Students in Teaching-Learning Reaction Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students have adequate foundations in modulation and visualization for understanding reaction mechanisms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students need support to visualize abstract molecular processes and represent them across macroscopic, microscopic, and symbolic levels.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should mentally or graphically map particle-level events to symbolic arrows and structures, aided by models or simulations.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students' poor foundations in modulation and visualization make teaching reaction mechanisms challenging"
misconceptions.prevalence: Reported qualitatively; no percentage given
misconceptions.source_title: Challenges Faced by Teachers and Students in Teaching-Learning Reaction Mechanism

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can understand reaction mechanisms without connecting them to experimental evidence.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Mechanistic explanations should be supported by experimental observations and evidence.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should use experimental results, rate data, and observed products to justify the proposed mechanism rather than relying only on memorization.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "One of the students' most significant difficulties is linking reaction mechanisms with experiments."
misconceptions.prevalence: Reported in conclusion; no percentage given
misconceptions.source_title: Challenges Faced by Teachers and Students in Teaching-Learning Reaction Mechanism

papers.paper_title: Development of Electronic Lab-book for College Chemistry-Experiment - SN1 & SN2 Reactions -

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think the SN1 reaction does not proceed through a carbocation intermediate, or do not understand that the intermediate is planar and can be attacked from either side.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In an SN1 reaction, the leaving group departs first to form a planar carbocation intermediate, and the nucleophile can attack from either side, often leading to racemization if the substrate is optically active.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that the reaction occurs in two steps: first ionization to a carbocation, then nucleophilic attack. Because the carbocation is trigonal planar, the nucleophile can approach from either face, so stereochemical scrambling/racemization can occur.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "In SN1 reactions ... a carbocation is first formed, which then reacts with the nucleophile. The carbocation is planar, and the anion can attack from either side."
misconceptions.population: University students in a basic organic chemistry course; practice session with four third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Development of Electronic Lab-book for College Chemistry-Experiment - SN1 & SN2 Reactions -

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think an SN1 reaction gives a single stereochemical product with retention of configuration rather than a racemic mixture.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: If the original substrate is optically active, SN1 reaction through a planar carbocation gives attack from either face and therefore a racemic mixture of products.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the planar intermediate with equal likelihood of attack on either side, which explains loss of optical purity and formation of racemate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Consequently, if the original molecule is optically active, a racemic mixture of products is obtained."
misconceptions.population: University students in a basic organic chemistry course
misconceptions.source_title: Development of Electronic Lab-book for College Chemistry-Experiment - SN1 & SN2 Reactions -

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think SN2 is not a concerted process, or may not know that the nucleophile attacks from one side while the leaving group departs from the opposite side.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: An SN2 reaction is concerted: bond formation and bond cleavage occur simultaneously, with backside attack by the nucleophile opposite the leaving group.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that the nucleophile approaches the electrophilic carbon as the leaving group leaves in one step; the geometry requires attack from the backside, opposite the leaving group, producing inversion.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the SN2 reaction ... is a concerted reaction in which the nucleophile approaches from the left side of the central carbon as the other group leaves to the right."
misconceptions.population: University students in a basic organic chemistry course; practice session with four third-year chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: Development of Electronic Lab-book for College Chemistry-Experiment - SN1 & SN2 Reactions -

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not know that SN2 causes inversion of configuration, or may think the product retains the original configuration.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN2 reactions proceed with inversion of configuration at the reacting stereocenter, known as Walden inversion.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from backside attack that the incoming nucleophile must displace the leaving group from the opposite side, flipping the three-dimensional arrangement and inverting configuration.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "In this case, the configuration of the molecule is inverted. ... an effect known as the Walden inversion"
misconceptions.population: University students in a basic organic chemistry course
misconceptions.source_title: Development of Electronic Lab-book for College Chemistry-Experiment - SN1 & SN2 Reactions -

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may confuse which reaction proceeds by stepwise carbocation formation versus which is concerted backside attack, or may not be able to distinguish SN1 from SN2 from textbook schemes alone.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN1 and SN2 have distinct mechanisms: SN1 is stepwise with a carbocation intermediate, while SN2 is concerted with backside attack and inversion.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the mechanistic sequence and stereochemical consequences: if there is a carbocation intermediate and possible racemization, it is SN1; if there is simultaneous bond-making/breaking and inversion, it is SN2.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "A schematic representation of the reaction is often used in textbooks, but it is not always easy for the student to obtain the configuration of the molecule or the dynamics of the reaction."
misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-test average 2.00/6.00, post-test average 5.25/6.00
misconceptions.population: Four third-year chemistry students of the teachers' training course at Tokyo Gakugei University
misconceptions.source_title: Development of Electronic Lab-book for College Chemistry-Experiment - SN1 & SN2 Reactions -

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not correctly interpret the reaction energy profile or understand energy change along the reaction coordinate for SN1 and SN2 reactions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reaction profiles show how potential energy changes during the reaction progress, including activation energy and transition-state region.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate the position on the reaction coordinate to molecular changes and recognize the energy barrier at the transition state and the overall energy change between reactants and products.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "After using the electronic lab-book, students' knowledge in terms of 'reactivity,' 'attacking direction,' and 'energy change' in the SN1 and SN2 reactions was improved."
misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-test: 0/6 correct on question 6 (reaction energy in SN1, SN2); post-test: 4/6 correct
misconceptions.population: Four third-year chemistry students of the teachers' training course at Tokyo Gakugei University
misconceptions.source_title: Development of Electronic Lab-book for College Chemistry-Experiment - SN1 & SN2 Reactions -

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not understand the attacking direction of the nucleophile in SN2, i.e. backside attack relative to the leaving group.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In SN2, the nucleophile approaches the central carbon from the side opposite the leaving group.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from orbital/geometric requirements that the nucleophile must attack from the backside to overlap properly and displace the leaving group in one step.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Figure 5: Quiz, Approaching Direction of Nucleophile to Central Carbon for SN2 Reaction in STEP 3."
misconceptions.prevalence: Pre-test: 3/6 correct on question 4 (attacking direction and product in SN2); post-test: 3/6 correct
misconceptions.population: Four third-year chemistry students of the teachers' training course at Tokyo Gakugei University
misconceptions.source_title: Development of Electronic Lab-book for College Chemistry-Experiment - SN1 & SN2 Reactions -

papers.paper_title: Comparing Nucleophilic Substitutions Versus Elimination Reactions in Comprehensive Introductory Organic Chemistry Textbooks

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot distinguish when nucleophilic substitution should be favored over elimination because they treat the two reaction classes as essentially the same or equally plausible in all cases.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nucleophilic substitution and elimination are competing pathways, and the dominant mechanism depends on substrate, reagent, and conditions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the reaction conditions and substrate features systematically, then decide whether substitution or elimination is more favorable under those conditions rather than assuming both are interchangeable.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Many students find the concept of nucleophilicity versus basicity confusing."
misconceptions.prevalence: "Many"; no numeric prevalence given
misconceptions.source_title: Comparing Nucleophilic Substitutions Versus Elimination Reactions in Comprehensive Introductory Organic Chemistry Textbooks

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students have difficulty predicting which pathway predominates when substitution and elimination are both possible under similar reaction conditions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The major pathway is determined by evaluating how substrate structure, nucleophile/base strength, temperature, and steric effects favor one mechanism over the other.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should weigh the relevant factors for the specific substrate and reagent set, then infer which mechanism is kinetically or thermodynamically favored in that situation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "predicting the predominant reaction"
misconceptions.prevalence: "Many" organic chemistry students; no numeric prevalence given
misconceptions.source_title: Comparing Nucleophilic Substitutions Versus Elimination Reactions in Comprehensive Introductory Organic Chemistry Textbooks

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students confuse nucleophilicity with basicity and do not distinguish the two when deciding between substitution and elimination.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nucleophilicity is a kinetic concept, while basicity is a thermodynamic concept; both must be considered separately in mechanism selection.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should ask whether the reagent is a better nucleophile or a stronger base, then connect nucleophilicity to substitution and basicity to elimination tendencies in the given context.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Some students find the concept of nucleophilicity versus basicity confusing."
misconceptions.prevalence: Some students; no numeric prevalence given
misconceptions.source_title: Comparing Nucleophilic Substitutions Versus Elimination Reactions in Comprehensive Introductory Organic Chemistry Textbooks

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not recognize that SN2 should be considered before SN1, and substitution before elimination, because they do not organize mechanisms from simpler to more complex.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN2 is generally introduced before SN1, and substitution before elimination, because the simpler mechanism helps build understanding of the more complex ones.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should learn and compare mechanisms in an order that starts with the simplest pathway and then moves to more complex competing pathways.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The SN2 mechanism is relatively straightforward and therefore should be presented before the SN1"
misconceptions.population: Textbook comparison; student misconception inferred from learning difficulty mentioned for undergraduates
misconceptions.source_title: Comparing Nucleophilic Substitutions Versus Elimination Reactions in Comprehensive Introductory Organic Chemistry Textbooks

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may fail to contrast substrate reactivity toward SN2 and SN1 using an ordered trend or may not see how the same substrate set can be ranked oppositely for the two mechanisms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Substrates should be ranked by how reactive they are toward SN2 and SN1, with trends showing opposite extremes for the two mechanisms.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the same series of substrates under both mechanisms and note that substrates most favorable for SN2 are least favorable for SN1, and vice versa.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The majority of texts examined herein compare the reactivity of substrates toward SN2 versus SN1 reactions by listing the substrates as a series."
misconceptions.prevalence: Majority of texts; no student percentage given
misconceptions.source_title: Comparing Nucleophilic Substitutions Versus Elimination Reactions in Comprehensive Introductory Organic Chemistry Textbooks

misconceptions.topic: SN2 vs E2 and SN1 vs E1
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not consider the full set of factors needed to choose between SN2 and E2 or between SN1 and E1, relying on only one or two cues.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Pathway selection should be based on multiple factors, especially base strength, temperature, steric effects, and nucleophilicity, because these competing reactions are similar in reagents and conditions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate all relevant determinants together rather than using a single shortcut, then decide which mechanism is most favored by the combination of factors.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Predicting whether nucleophilic substitution or elimination predominates in these reactions eludes many organic chemistry students"
misconceptions.prevalence: "many" organic chemistry students; no numeric prevalence given
misconceptions.source_title: Comparing Nucleophilic Substitutions Versus Elimination Reactions in Comprehensive Introductory Organic Chemistry Textbooks

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may not understand that Zaitsev and Hofmann rules are part of E2 elimination and are needed to predict the alkene product regiochemistry.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Zaitsev and Hofmann eliminations are subcases of E2 that help predict the regio- and stereochemistry of the alkene product.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should determine which alkene is favored by applying Zaitsev or Hofmann reasoning within an E2 framework, using substrate and reagent features to predict the major product.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Zaitsev rules and Hofmann rules predict the regio- and stereochemistry of the new double bond resulting from E2 elimination."
misconceptions.source_title: Comparing Nucleophilic Substitutions Versus Elimination Reactions in Comprehensive Introductory Organic Chemistry Textbooks

misconceptions.subtopic: Determinants of Zaitsev vs Hofmann outcome
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may rely on only one criterion, such as steric hindrance, when deciding between Zaitsev and Hofmann elimination, instead of considering multiple determinants.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The Zaitsev vs Hofmann outcome depends on substrate steric requirements, carbanion stability, proton acidity, and leaving-group basicity.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should analyze all four determinants and use them together to infer whether the more substituted alkene or the Hofmann product is preferred.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Comparing the Zaitsev and the Hofmann eliminations uses substrate steric requirements, carbanion stability, proton acidity, and leaving group basicity as regiochemical determinants"
misconceptions.source_title: Comparing Nucleophilic Substitutions Versus Elimination Reactions in Comprehensive Introductory Organic Chemistry Textbooks

papers.paper_title: ASSESSMENT OF UNDERGRADUATE CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN ORGANIC CHEMISTRY

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot correctly identify or apply the reaction chemistry of functional groups when asked to write reactions, syntheses, or mechanisms; their answers lack coherent step-by-step chemical reasoning.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A correct solution requires recognizing the functional group, its typical reactivity, and using appropriate reagents and a logical mechanism to transform starting materials into products.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: First identify the functional groups present and the target functional group. Then determine the relevant reaction type and choose suitable reagents/conditions. Finally, write a coherent stepwise mechanism that accounts for bond changes and product formation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "most of the students' answers showed lack of organization (coherence), and also without algorithms or step by step problem solving approach."
misconceptions.prevalence: 164/177 (92.65%) could not give appropriate and right answers on the functional-groups synthesis question
misconceptions.source_title: ASSESSMENT OF UNDERGRADUATE CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN ORGANIC CHEMISTRY

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students determine the R/S sequence incorrectly by tracing priorities from 1 to 2 to 3 instead of orienting the lowest-priority group to the rear and tracing 1 to 2 to 4.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: R/S assignment uses Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority rules: with the lowest-priority group pointing away, the 1→2→3 direction determines R or S; if the lowest-priority group is not away, the molecule must be reoriented or corrected by interchange rules.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Assign priorities to the substituents, place the lowest priority group behind the stereocenter, then trace the sequence 1→2→3 to determine the configuration according to CIP rules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "majority of students started from 1 and moved to 2 through 3 rather than starting from 1 and move to 2 through 4."
misconceptions.prevalence: 158/177 (89.26%) had difficulty visualizing and addressing the spatial orientation of the molecule
misconceptions.source_title: ASSESSMENT OF UNDERGRADUATE CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN ORGANIC CHEMISTRY

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot reliably identify axial and equatorial positions or decide the most stable chair conformation of cis- and trans-disubstituted cyclohexanes.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Conformation stability depends on whether substituents occupy axial or equatorial positions; the most stable conformation minimizes steric strain, especially placing bulky groups equatorial when possible.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Draw both chair conformations, locate axial and equatorial positions, then compare steric interactions. Choose the conformation with the least strain and explain stability in terms of substituent placement.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Majority of students have difficulty in identify the axial and equatorial positions for different conformations of di-substituted cyclohexane"
misconceptions.prevalence: 152/177 (85.87%) failed to give the appropriate structural formula for the most stable conformation
misconceptions.source_title: ASSESSMENT OF UNDERGRADUATE CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN ORGANIC CHEMISTRY

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not correctly visualize stereoisomers in three dimensions or relate 2-D drawings to 3-D molecular structures.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different three-dimensional arrangements, and students must mentally represent and compare those spatial structures.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Interpret the 2-D representation as a 3-D object, identify how substituents are oriented in space, and use that spatial model to compare or classify stereoisomers.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "many students have difficulties in visualizing structures of stereoisomers in three-dimensional forms; in relating three-dimensional with two-dimensional shapes"
misconceptions.population: undergraduate Chemistry students / 177 first year Chemistry students
misconceptions.source_title: ASSESSMENT OF UNDERGRADUATE CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN ORGANIC CHEMISTRY

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot correctly classify organic reactions as substitution, elimination, addition, or rearrangement, nor write the corresponding mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should identify the reaction type from the substrates, reagents, and conditions, then use the appropriate mechanistic pathway to explain product formation.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Examine the reactant structure and reaction conditions, determine whether the change is substitution, elimination, addition, or rearrangement, and then draw the mechanism consistent with that reaction class.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students have difficulty in giving appropriate answers in organic reaction and mechanisms topics."
misconceptions.prevalence: Only 11/177 (6.21%) gave appropriate answer; 104/177 (58.75%) scored 1 or less out of 3
misconceptions.source_title: ASSESSMENT OF UNDERGRADUATE CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN ORGANIC CHEMISTRY

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot correctly explain the dehydration of 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol to 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, including the need to write the correct formula, conditions, and elimination mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Under acidic conditions, dehydration of the alcohol proceeds by the appropriate elimination mechanism to yield the alkene product, with correct structural representation and mechanistic steps.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Write the alcohol structure correctly, identify the reaction as acid-catalyzed dehydration, then show the elimination mechanism leading to the stated alkene product under the given conditions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Dehydration of 3, 3-dimethylbutan-2-ol results in the formation of 2, 3 dimethylbut-2-ene as the major product. Write the equation and show the mechanism of reaction clearly."
misconceptions.source_title: ASSESSMENT OF UNDERGRADUATE CHEMISTRY STUDENTS' DIFFICULTIES IN ORGANIC CHEMISTRY

papers.paper_title: Energy Profiles and Transition States in Organic Reactions: A Computational Study

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students view reaction coordinate diagrams as static pictures rather than representations of molecular motion and change along the reaction path.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reaction coordinate diagrams represent the energetic progression of a reaction as molecular structures change dynamically from reactants to products.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should interpret the horizontal axis as reaction progress and the vertical axis as energy, recognizing that points on the diagram correspond to changing structures and energies along the pathway, not fixed isolated objects.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Many students incorrectly view reaction coordinate diagrams as static rather than dynamic representations of molecular motion"
misconceptions.source_title: Energy Profiles and Transition States in Organic Reactions: A Computational Study

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students misinterpret reaction coordinate diagrams and thereby confuse activation energy with reaction spontaneity.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Activation energy is the energy barrier that must be overcome for a reaction to proceed; spontaneity is determined by thermodynamic factors, not by the size of the activation barrier alone.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish kinetic concepts from thermodynamic ones: a reaction can have a high or low activation energy regardless of whether it is spontaneous, and spontaneity depends on free-energy change.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "leading to misinterpretation of activation energy and reaction spontaneity"
misconceptions.source_title: Energy Profiles and Transition States in Organic Reactions: A Computational Study

misconceptions.subtopic: Stationary points on the potential energy surface
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students confuse intermediates with transition states.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermediates are local minima on the potential energy surface, whereas transition states are maxima corresponding to transient configurations.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify intermediates as relatively stable species that may exist between steps and transition states as the highest-energy points that connect minima; a transition state cannot be isolated as a stable species.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Another common error involves confusing intermediates with transition states"
misconceptions.source_title: Energy Profiles and Transition States in Organic Reactions: A Computational Study

misconceptions.subtopic: Isolation and stability of transition states
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat transition states as if they were ordinary species that can be isolated like intermediates.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Transition states are fleeting, high-energy configurations and are not isolable under normal conditions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that a species at a maximum on the reaction coordinate is not a stable minimum; therefore it cannot be bottled or isolated, only inferred computationally or indirectly.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the latter are energy maxima representing transient configurations that cannot be isolated"
misconceptions.source_title: Energy Profiles and Transition States in Organic Reactions: A Computational Study

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume computed energy minima and maxima are static structures rather than dynamic states influenced by vibrational and entropic effects.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Minima and maxima on a potential energy surface are approximations to structures along a reaction pathway and real systems also involve vibrational motion and entropy.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect the PES to molecular motion: a minimum corresponds to a stable structure, but the actual molecule still vibrates and its behavior is affected by entropy and temperature.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "many assume that computed energy minima and maxima represent static structures"
misconceptions.source_title: Energy Profiles and Transition States in Organic Reactions: A Computational Study

papers.paper_title: Functional Group Transformations in Organic Chemistry: Reactivity and Selectivity

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat functional groups as isolated entities and ignore the influence of the rest of the molecule on reactivity and selectivity.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Functional groups behave as part of an interdependent electronic system whose reactivity depends on the molecular context.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that substituents, electronic effects, steric effects, and the surrounding molecular framework alter electron density and therefore change how a functional group reacts.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Many learners mistakenly interpret functional groups as isolated entities rather than as interdependent electronic systems influenced by molecular context.”
misconceptions.source_title: Functional Group Transformations in Organic Chemistry: Reactivity and Selectivity

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students confuse kinetic control with thermodynamic control when predicting products in reversible reactions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Kinetic control favors the fastest-forming product, while thermodynamic control favors the most stable product under equilibrium conditions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify whether the reaction is under kinetic or thermodynamic conditions by considering temperature, reversibility, and equilibration, then predict the appropriate product accordingly.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Another common error lies in confusing kinetic and thermodynamic control, particularly when predicting product ratios in reversible reactions.”
misconceptions.source_title: Functional Group Transformations in Organic Chemistry: Reactivity and Selectivity

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students conflate SN1 and SN2 mechanisms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN1 and SN2 are distinct substitution mechanisms with different rate laws, intermediates, stereochemical outcomes, and substrate preferences.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the substrate structure, nucleophile strength, solvent, and stereochemical evidence to determine whether a reaction proceeds by SN1 or SN2.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Misapplication of mechanistic models—such as conflating SN1 with SN2 processes...”
misconceptions.source_title: Functional Group Transformations in Organic Chemistry: Reactivity and Selectivity

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students misunderstand electrophilic addition mechanisms.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrophilic addition follows specific mechanistic steps involving attack by an electrophile on a π system and subsequent formation of intermediates/products according to the substrate and conditions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should analyze the π bond, identify the electrophile and nucleophile roles, and trace electron movement step by step rather than memorizing the reaction name only.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Misapplication of mechanistic models—such as conflating SN1 with SN2 processes or misunderstanding electrophilic addition mechanisms—further complicates comprehension.”
misconceptions.source_title: Functional Group Transformations in Organic Chemistry: Reactivity and Selectivity

papers.paper_title: Analysis of Common Conceptual Errors of CCP Questions

misconceptions.subtopic: Leaving group departure vs carbocation formation
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the halide leaves first to form a carbocation intermediate, leading them to apply an SN1-like pathway in an acyl substitution reaction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In nucleophilic acyl substitution, the nucleophile attacks the acyl carbon to form a tetrahedral intermediate; the leaving group is expelled from that intermediate, not by prior carbocation formation.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Recognize the carbonyl carbon as the electrophile, add the nucleophile to form the tetrahedral intermediate, then collapse the intermediate to expel the leaving group. Do not generate a carbocation at the acyl carbon.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "26.9% of them expelled the bromo-halide group first which created a highly unstable carbocation in intermediate 1."
misconceptions.prevalence: 26.9% of students who answered October 19th incorrectly; 91 students made an SN1-type conceptual error
misconceptions.population: 524 students total; 432 analyzed for October 19th question
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of Common Conceptual Errors of CCP Questions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students fail to dissociate the anionic nucleophile salt (e.g., NaO2CCH3 or NaOCH3) before using it in the mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A salt nucleophile should be recognized as dissociated in solution, with the reactive anion acting as the nucleophile and sodium as a spectator ion.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify the salt as an ionic compound in solution, separate it into ions, and use the anion as the nucleophile while leaving out the counterion from the electron-pushing steps.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "About 21.7% of students who completed the activity did not recognize that NaO2CCH3 was a salt that could easily be dissociated in an aqueous solution."
misconceptions.prevalence: 21.7% on October 19th; 23.4% on October 21st failed to dissociate the nucleophile
misconceptions.population: October 19th: students who completed the activity; October 21st: students who completed the activity
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of Common Conceptual Errors of CCP Questions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not use the acid catalyst in the mechanism, implying they do not recognize that the reaction is acid-catalyzed or do not connect the given conditions to the mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Under acidic conditions, the mechanism must include protonation steps that activate the electrophile and facilitate subsequent substitution steps.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use the H+ condition to protonate the appropriate oxygen or carbonyl site first, then proceed with nucleophilic attack and later deprotonation steps.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The most frequent mistake with this mechanism was failure to use the acid catalyst when carrying out the reaction."
misconceptions.prevalence: 56.0% of students who completed October 26th made this error
misconceptions.population: October 26th CCP question; 459 student assignments analyzed
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of Common Conceptual Errors of CCP Questions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students protonate the wrong oxygen in the initial protonation step, often the hydroxyl group farther from the carbonyl or the carboxylic-acid hydroxyl group.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The correct protonation site is the oxygen that best activates the electrophile for the intramolecular substitution pathway shown by the mechanism.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Inspect the functional groups and choose the oxygen whose protonation makes the best leaving group and leads to the intended intramolecular cyclization/substitution pathway.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The most frequent conceptual error made by students in this question was during the initial protonation step where students had difficulty in choosing the correct protonation site."
misconceptions.prevalence: 18.6% protonated the wrong oxygen; among those, 68.0% protonated the hydroxyl farther from the carbonyl and 31.9% protonated the carboxylic-acid hydroxyl
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of Common Conceptual Errors of CCP Questions

misconceptions.subtopic: Dehydration or attack after incorrect protonation
misconceptions.target_misconception: After protonating the wrong hydroxyl, students either let that protonated hydroxyl leave without nucleophilic attack or perform nucleophilic attack on the incorrectly protonated intermediate.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Once the correct site is protonated, the mechanism should proceed through the intended nucleophilic attack and subsequent elimination steps; dehydration should not be shown as a substitute pathway here.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: First protonate the correct oxygen to create the right leaving group, then follow the specific intramolecular substitution sequence rather than ejecting water prematurely or attacking the wrong intermediate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The most common erroneous mechanistic path that students took after that point was either one of two routes: they performed a nucleophilic attack which expels either a protonated or nonprotonated hydroxyl group ... or made the protonated hydroxyl group leave without a nucleophilic attack (dehydration)."
misconceptions.prevalence: About one third chose the nucleophilic attack route and another third chose the dehydration route among those making the protonation-site error
misconceptions.population: Students who made the protonation-site error on October 28th
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of Common Conceptual Errors of CCP Questions

misconceptions.subtopic: Order of elimination in tetrahedral intermediate collapse
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students eliminate the amine group without simultaneously forming the carbonyl C=O bond, treating these as separate rather than concerted events.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When the tetrahedral intermediate collapses, the C=O bond reforms as the leaving group departs in the same step.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Recognize the collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate as a coupled electron-flow step: electrons from oxygen form the carbonyl while the amine leaves at the same time.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Close to 15% of students eliminated the amine group without simultaneous formation of the C-O double bond."
misconceptions.prevalence: Close to 15%
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of Common Conceptual Errors of CCP Questions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students deprotonate the hydroxyl group of the intermediate before the elimination step instead of collapsing the intermediate first.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The hydroxyl-bearing intermediate must collapse appropriately to re-form the carbonyl before or as leaving-group departure occurs; simple deprotonation alone is not the correct next step.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Follow the mechanism sequence: activate the intermediate as needed, then allow electron flow to reform the C=O and expel the leaving group rather than stopping after deprotonation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "about 10% of students simply just deprotonated the hydroxyl group of intermediate 3 before the elimination step"
misconceptions.prevalence: About 10%
misconceptions.concept_category: proton transfer / step order in mechanism
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of Common Conceptual Errors of CCP Questions

misconceptions.subtopic: Ignoring stereochemistry at the anomeric carbon
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not indicate stereochemistry in the key intermediate and/or final product, treating the anomeric center as if stereochemistry does not matter.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The anomeric carbon can be attacked from either face, so stereochemistry must be shown because it determines the axial/equatorial outcome and possible racemic products.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Track the 3D configuration at the anomeric center, indicate whether attack occurs from the front or back, and draw the corresponding stereochemical outcome in the intermediate and product.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "One of the most common concepts lacking in this question was the indication of stereochemistry within intermediate 4 of the mechanism"
misconceptions.prevalence: 75.5% of students who obtained a wrong intermediate 4 lacked stereochemistry indication; 31.6% of those also had correct final product stereochemistry
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of Common Conceptual Errors of CCP Questions

misconceptions.subtopic: Not indicating formal charge on intermediates
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students omit formal charges on intermediates, even when the charged species should be shown.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermediates should display the correct formal charges wherever charge is present in the mechanism.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: After each protonation/deprotonation or bond-making/bond-breaking step, assign formal charges to atoms according to valence and electron count, and show them in the drawn intermediate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "there was an increase in incidences of the lack of formal charges as the mechanism progresses"
misconceptions.prevalence: Trend observed across intermediates; exact percentage not given in text
misconceptions.population: November 23rd CCP question; intermediates attempted by students
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of Common Conceptual Errors of CCP Questions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students draw an arrow starting from hydrogen or the wrong atom instead of from the oxygen lone pair/bond electrons during deprotonation.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electron-pushing arrows must start at the electron source, such as the O-H bond or an oxygen lone pair, and end at the atom or bond receiving electrons.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify where electrons are located, start the arrow at that bond or lone pair, and point it to the correct atom so the deprotonation step reflects actual electron movement.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "there was a 'wrong source, right end' point in a deprotonation step."
misconceptions.prevalence: Frequency not quantified; described as a frequent error
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of Common Conceptual Errors of CCP Questions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students remove an incorrect α-hydrogen, producing an unlikely or unstable ring-containing product.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Base should remove the α-hydrogen that leads to the correct enolate and the most plausible aldol condensation product.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Compare the available α-hydrogens, choose the one that gives the reactive enolate/enol consistent with the product pathway, and avoid generating highly strained or implausible cyclic products.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "About 17.7% of students had deprotonated the wrong hydrogen, which usually lead to highly unlikely and unstable four and seven membered ring structures."
misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of Common Conceptual Errors of CCP Questions

papers.paper_title: Heteroatom Substitutions in Organic Frameworks: Effects on Reactivity and Function

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe heteroatom incorporation always enhances reactivity or selectivity.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Heteroatom substitution can either increase or decrease reactivity/selectivity depending on electronic, steric, and environmental factors.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate the specific heteroatom, its position, and the reaction conditions, then consider inductive, resonance, and steric effects before predicting whether reactivity or selectivity will improve.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: “A common misconception is that heteroatom incorporation always enhances reactivity or selectivity”
misconceptions.source_title: Heteroatom Substitutions in Organic Frameworks: Effects on Reactivity and Function

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think electronegativity alone determines substituent effects.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Substituent effects are determined by multiple factors, including resonance, hybridization, molecular environment, and electronegativity.
