misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should analyze the actual reagent and solvent interactions, then relate those to nucleophile/base behavior and mechanism choice.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "In this situation, hydrogen bonding is not possible. So that leaves SN2, E2."
misconceptions.prevalence: Individual student example; not quantified.
misconceptions.source_title: What are they seeing? How students predict and explain substitution and elimination reactions

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe a larger nucleophile/base automatically implies SN1 because it is too large to react in one step.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular size alone does not determine whether a reaction proceeds by SN1, SN2, E1, or E2; substrate structure and reagent strength/function matter.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should evaluate steric hindrance, nucleophile strength, and substrate substitution rather than using size as a standalone rule.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "because, as she later explains, compounds that are too large cannot substitute in one step and need a second step to attack"
misconceptions.prevalence: Individual student example; not quantified.
misconceptions.source_title: What are they seeing? How students predict and explain substitution and elimination reactions

papers.paper_title: Using Stop Motion Animations to Activate and Analyze High School Students' Intuitive Resources about Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think SN1 and SN2 are not competing alternative mechanisms for the same reaction, but instead propose only one pathway and do not consider that both could be possible.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For a given reaction, more than one mechanistic pathway can be possible in principle; SN1 and SN2 are alternative mechanisms that may both occur depending on conditions and substrate.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare conditions, substrate structure, and kinetics to determine whether a stepwise or concerted pathway is more plausible, and recognize that mechanistic alternatives can coexist as possibilities rather than forcing a single absolute answer.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "no group discussed whether both mechanisms could be possible"
misconceptions.prevalence: 0 groups out of 19 groups in Data Collection C explicitly discussed both mechanisms as possible
misconceptions.population: 55 German high school students (23 groups overall; 19 groups evaluated the pre-made SMAs)
misconceptions.source_title: Using Stop Motion Animations to Activate and Analyze High School Students' Intuitive Resources about Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think reaction steps should happen one after another rather than simultaneously; concerted movement of nucleophile and leaving group is avoided or not recognized.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In an SN2 mechanism, nucleophile attack and leaving-group departure occur at the same time in a concerted process.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason that bond formation and bond breaking can be coupled in one elementary step, so the nucleophile approaches as the leaving group departs simultaneously.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The simultaneous movement of Br and O is thus completely avoided."
misconceptions.prevalence: 4 SMAs in category X showed simultaneous movement; 6 SMAs in BA showed sequential movement; 10 SMAs in BX/BA showed O approach and Br departure, but often not simultaneously
misconceptions.source_title: Using Stop Motion Animations to Activate and Analyze High School Students' Intuitive Resources about Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the nucleophile attacks from the same side where the leaving group is attached, rather than from the backside.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN2 reactions proceed by backside attack due to steric/electrostatic requirements, leading to inversion at the carbon center.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should consider spatial arrangement and steric repulsion, and reason that the nucleophile approaches opposite the leaving group to allow bond formation while the leaving group leaves.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "In contrast, in all student-generated SMAs, O approaches from the same side of the black ball that Br is bound to."
misconceptions.prevalence: All student-generated SN2-like SMAs showed same-side approach; backside attack was never shown
misconceptions.source_title: Using Stop Motion Animations to Activate and Analyze High School Students' Intuitive Resources about Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students ignore or do not expect any movement of hydrogen atoms during carbocation formation or nucleophilic attack.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When molecular geometry changes during reaction, attached hydrogens may reposition as the bonding environment changes; mechanistic representations should account for all atom movements relevant to the structure change.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should track the geometry of the whole molecule, not only the leaving group and nucleophile, and recognize that all substituents on the carbon can change position when the central geometry changes.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "none of the student-generated SMAs—except those in the 'OTHER' category that depict bond cleavage—shows any movement of the Hs."
misconceptions.prevalence: Hydrogen movement was not shown in the student-generated SMAs except in the OTHER category
misconceptions.source_title: Using Stop Motion Animations to Activate and Analyze High School Students' Intuitive Resources about Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think bonding can happen only at fixed, pre-existing 'places' or 'sites' on the atom surface, so a new bond must form exactly where another bond was removed.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond formation is determined by molecular orbital/electrostatic interactions and geometry, not by fixed surface 'slots'; in SN2, the nucleophile approaches from the backside while the leaving group departs.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason from 3D molecular geometry and electron distribution, recognizing that atom surfaces do not contain fixed bond sockets and that reactive approach direction matters.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "many students somehow expect bonding to 'happen' only at specific places on an atomic surface."
misconceptions.prevalence: 6 groups discussed 'bonding sites' or fixed places for bonds
misconceptions.population: 14 groups mentioned chemical bonds in any context during Data Collection C
misconceptions.source_title: Using Stop Motion Animations to Activate and Analyze High School Students' Intuitive Resources about Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a carbon atom cannot transiently have five bonds, so any mechanism with five bonds is impossible.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In an SN2 reaction, the transition state can involve partial bonds and an apparent five-coordinate arrangement; the octet rule applies to stable structures, not necessarily to transition states.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish stable intermediates from transition states and understand that temporary bond formation/breaking can produce a high-energy arrangement that is not a stable pentavalent carbon compound.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "temporarily there are five bonds"
misconceptions.prevalence: 4 groups focused on the number of chemical bonds; this argument was used both for and against SN2 mechanisms
misconceptions.population: 14 groups mentioned chemical bonds in any context
misconceptions.concept_category: oxidation numbers / octet rule / bonding count
misconceptions.source_title: Using Stop Motion Animations to Activate and Analyze High School Students' Intuitive Resources about Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think bromine leaving without an obvious external cause is unrealistic or impossible, so a stepwise SN1-like departure seems implausible.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Leaving-group departure can occur because of internal energetic and electronic factors and stabilization by the environment; a visible external 'cause' is not always required in the model of the elementary step.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should reason from energetic favorability, bond polarization, and stabilization of the developing ion rather than from everyday 'cause-and-effect' expectations alone.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it is not 'realistic' that bromine would leave 'just like that'"
misconceptions.prevalence: 12 groups judged probability by plausibility; this argument was only used against SN1
misconceptions.population: 19 groups that evaluated the pre-made SMAs
misconceptions.source_title: Using Stop Motion Animations to Activate and Analyze High School Students' Intuitive Resources about Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat alternative reaction pathways mainly as different intermediate-containing pathways rather than recognizing that concerted pathways can be alternatives too.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Alternative mechanistic pathways can differ in whether they proceed stepwise or concertedly; not all alternatives require a distinct intermediate.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should compare whether bond making and bond breaking happen together or in separate steps and should not assume that every alternative route must feature a new intermediate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students thinking about alternative reaction pathways first of all think about other intermediates"
misconceptions.prevalence: 7 of 32 SMAs were in the OTHER category; 5 of these involved intermediates
misconceptions.source_title: Using Stop Motion Animations to Activate and Analyze High School Students' Intuitive Resources about Reaction Mechanisms

papers.paper_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that organic chemistry is inherently too difficult to understand or succeed in.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Organic chemistry can be learned successfully with effective instruction, practice, and support; difficulty does not mean impossibility.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should treat difficulty as a sign to seek strategies such as early practice, help-seeking, and concept review rather than assuming they cannot learn the subject.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students still have difficulty understanding and comprehending the subject material"
misconceptions.population: undergraduate students in organic chemistry (general discussion in the paper)
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: Educators/students believe that instruction should be matched to a student's preferred learning style (visual, auditory, tactile) for effective learning.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The learning styles theory is not supported by empirical evidence; instruction should not be tailored on the assumption that students learn best only through one style.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that people can learn through multiple modes and that evidence does not justify assigning instruction by claimed learning style.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The theory of learning styles posits that there are specific ways that students learn best."
misconceptions.population: educators and students discussed in the review of learning styles research
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that if a lesson does not match their learning style, they will not learn as effectively.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students can learn effectively through different instructional methods; matching instruction to a claimed learning style does not improve learning outcomes in the evidence cited.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should focus on engaging with the material and using multiple approaches rather than assuming only one preferred mode will work.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Theoretically, if a student learns best through one method, then they should not be able to learn as effectively using other methods."
misconceptions.population: participants in learning-styles research discussed in the paper
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe intelligence is fixed and cannot be improved with effort.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intelligence can improve with effort, practice, and perseverance; a growth mindset is beneficial.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret difficulty as something to work through and improve upon rather than as proof of a permanent limit.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "those with a fixed mindset feel that intelligence is a fixed trait that cannot be improved"
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that struggling in a subject means they are not smart or capable enough to understand it.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Struggle is part of learning; students can become capable through persistence, practice, and support.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should attribute setbacks to the need for more practice or better strategies, not to a lack of innate ability.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students can begin to think that they are just not smart or capable enough to understand such material."
misconceptions.population: students in traditional learning environments (general discussion)
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: People believe gamers typically play because they are lonely, have low self-esteem, or want to escape a miserable life.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Gaming motivations are varied and often social, competitive, or enjoyable rather than reflecting social dysfunction.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should avoid inferring personality deficits from gaming and instead consider the diversity of motives for play.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "those who lacked friendships, had low self-esteem, and looked to the internet as a means to escape a miserable life"
misconceptions.population: internet users/gamers as discussed in cited stereotype literature
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can succeed in organic chemistry without properly understanding foundational general chemistry topics such as acid-base chemistry, orbital hybridization, bonding, Lewis dot structures, and 3-D structures.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Success in organic chemistry depends on understanding these foundational concepts first.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect organic chemistry mechanisms and structures back to prerequisite chemistry ideas before trying to memorize reactions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students will face many challenges throughout the rest of the course"
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think SN1 and SN2 reactions are simple to understand once they are shown the reactions, without needing to sort through the reactants, products, and variations carefully.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN1 and SN2 mechanisms must be determined from the specific reactants, substrates, and conditions; the mechanism is not obvious without analysis.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare substrate structure, nucleophile, leaving group, and conditions to decide which substitution pathway applies.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "It is pretty simple to understand what happens in the reactions once one determines which types of reaction takes place."
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think E1 and E2 elimination reactions are essentially the same as SN1 and SN2 substitution reactions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: E1 and E2 are elimination reactions and differ from substitution reactions in mechanism and products.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish whether the reaction removes groups to form a double bond or substitutes one group for another, then analyze the mechanism accordingly.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "E1 and E2 reactions are similar to S1 and S2 except they are two different kinds of elimination reactions."
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think nomenclature is mainly about memorizing word parts rather than using them to systematically name structures by reading structural changes.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nomenclature is a systematic naming process based on recognizing structure, functional groups, and how changes in a molecule alter its name.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the structural features of a molecule and apply naming rules rather than rely on rote memorization alone.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "It can be difficult for students to remember word parts."
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think Lewis dot structures can be drawn and understood without correctly accounting for valence electrons.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lewis dot structures require correct counting and placement of valence electrons.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first determine the total valence electrons and then distribute them according to bonding and lone-pair rules to make a correct Lewis structure.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Without a proper understanding of valence electrons, lewis dot structures can be difficult to create and understand."
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think 3-D molecular structures can be understood easily from 2-D drawings without needing to visualize the molecule in three dimensions.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students must mentally transform and visualize structures in three dimensions from 2-D representations.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use spatial reasoning to interpret wedge/dash or other projections and connect 2-D depictions to the actual 3-D arrangement.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Organic chemistry requires spatial intelligence in understanding how 3D structures look when drawn in 2D."
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think functional groups are just add-ons to benzene rings and may not realize that adding them changes both structure and name.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Functional groups are structural features whose presence and position affect a molecule's structure and nomenclature.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the functional group, determine where it is attached, and then apply the naming rules that reflect that structural change.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "When a functional group is added to a benzene ring, its name changes."
misconceptions.source_title: Game-Based Learning in Science: Can Video Games Simplify Organic Chemistry?

papers.paper_title: Getting Past the Rules and to the WHY: Causal Mechanistic Arguments When Judging the Plausibility of Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students judge an SN1 reaction mainly by steric hindrance of the starting material, treating tertiary steric bulk as the reason a pathway is favored or disfavored in this SN1 context.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For SN1 plausibility, the key evidence is carbocation stability and the resulting activation energy of the rate-determining step, not steric hindrance of the starting material.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Compare the two substrates in terms of the stability of the carbocation intermediate that would form. A more stable carbocation lowers the activation energy for the rate-determining step, making the SN1 pathway more likely.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Incorrect claims were often supported by causal arguments but these arguments were incorrectly based on drawing a causal relationship between the relative steric hindrance of the starting materials and activation energy."
misconceptions.prevalence: Incorrect claims were often supported this way; the paper does not give a percentage for this misconception.
misconceptions.source_title: Getting Past the Rules and to the WHY: Causal Mechanistic Arguments When Judging the Plausibility of Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students use a memorized rule that tertiary alkyl halides react via SN1 and primary alkyl halides react via SN2, without reasoning about why the mechanism is favored in the specific problem.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should justify mechanism choice by reasoning from relevant mechanistic factors, especially carbocation stability and activation energy for SN1, rather than only applying a surface rule.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Use the reaction features to explain why a particular intermediate or transition state is more or less favorable. For SN1, explain that a tertiary substrate forms a more stable carbocation and therefore has a lower activation barrier than a primary substrate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "These arguments were rule-based in nature, generally explaining that tertiary alkyl halides react via an $S_N1$ mechanism while primary alkyl halides react via an $S_N2$ mechanism, without giving a reason why."
misconceptions.prevalence: Reported as one of the two common relational argument forms; no percentage given for this specific misconception.
misconceptions.source_title: Getting Past the Rules and to the WHY: Causal Mechanistic Arguments When Judging the Plausibility of Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a tertiary carbocation is more stable than a primary carbocation but do not connect that stability to a cause, such as hyperconjugation.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Tertiary carbocations are more stable because adjacent alkyl groups donate electron density through hyperconjugation; primary carbocations have fewer such stabilizing interactions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Compare the number of adjacent C–H sigma bonds available for hyperconjugation. More adjacent methyl groups means more overlap with the empty p orbital, greater stabilization, and thus greater carbocation stability.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Few arguments invoked hyperconjugation to explain why the tertiary carbocation is more stable than the primary; in other words, few arguments went down to the expected level of granularity."
misconceptions.prevalence: Few arguments invoked hyperconjugation; the paper does not report an exact percentage.
misconceptions.source_title: Getting Past the Rules and to the WHY: Causal Mechanistic Arguments When Judging the Plausibility of Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students explain the activation energy difference by saying it takes less energy to form a tertiary carbocation than a primary carbocation, without explicitly linking that to carbocation stability or to the transition state of the rate-determining step.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Activation energy is connected to transition-state energy; for SN1, the transition state resembles the carbocation-like species, so greater carbocation stability lowers the activation barrier.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Reason from Hammond's postulate: because the rate-determining step is endergonic, the transition state resembles the carbocation intermediate. A more stable carbocation corresponds to a lower-energy transition state and a lower activation energy.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The other common relational argument discussed carbocation substitution and either energy or activation energy, generally explaining that it takes less energy to form a tertiary carbocation than a primary carbocation, without invoking stability as a cause."
misconceptions.prevalence: Described as one of the two common relational argument forms; no percentage given for this specific misconception.
misconceptions.source_title: Getting Past the Rules and to the WHY: Causal Mechanistic Arguments When Judging the Plausibility of Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students argue that steric hindrance makes the activation energy barrier to product formation in reaction B higher, even though the prompt states both reactions proceed by SN1.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For the SN1 comparison in this question, the correct pathway is determined by carbocation stability and the associated activation barrier, not by steric hindrance leading to an SN2-style rationale.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify the relevant SN1 features, compare the carbocation intermediates that would form, and use their relative stability to infer the activation energy for the rate-determining step.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the most common causal argument was centered on the idea of steric hindrance, which was incorrectly used to justify why the activation energy barrier to the formation of the product in reaction B would be higher"
misconceptions.prevalence: The most common causal argument for incorrect claims; no exact percentage given.
misconceptions.source_title: Getting Past the Rules and to the WHY: Causal Mechanistic Arguments When Judging the Plausibility of Organic Reaction Mechanisms

papers.paper_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Curved arrows are just a means to get from reactants to products and have no physical meaning.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Curved arrows represent electron flow and are meant to explain the mechanistic process by which reactants are transformed into products.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret each arrow as showing movement of electrons from a source to a sink and use it to justify why each bond breaks or forms in a chemically plausible sequence.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The curved arrows used in the electron-pushing formalism held no physical meaning for the graduate students involved in this study."
misconceptions.prevalence: described as the dominant pattern across the participants; no exact percentage given
misconceptions.population: 14 graduate students in a first-semester graduate-level organic chemistry course
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think mechanism solving is just 'playing around' or forcing steps until they fit the product.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Mechanism proposal should be based on chemically justified electron flow and reaction principles, not trial-and-error forcing.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should test whether each proposed step is consistent with reactivity, charge movement, and known mechanistic pathways before accepting it.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "It's basically just playing around"
misconceptions.population: Graduate students interviewed in the study
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students will accept nonsensical or highly unstable intermediates if those intermediates seem to lead toward the product.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Intermediates must be chemically reasonable and consistent with reaction energetics and known mechanisms.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reject intermediates that are too unstable or incompatible with the reaction conditions, even if they superficially connect reactants to products.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "all of the participants generated the highly unstable phenyl cation intermediate"
misconceptions.prevalence: all of the participants
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think protonation should occur on the ester oxygen rather than the carbonyl oxygen in ester saponification.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In these reactions, protonation of the carbonyl oxygen is expected because it better stabilizes the resulting cationic intermediate.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the site where protonation gives the more stabilized cation and better activates the substrate for subsequent reaction.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Most of the participants in this study protonated the ester oxygen in both questions that dealt with ester saponification reactions. Protonation at the carbonyl oxygen, however, would have been expected in both cases"
misconceptions.prevalence: most of the participants; exact percentage not given
misconceptions.population: Graduate students interviewed on two ester saponification problems
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat an ester as a carbonyl attached to an ether rather than as a single functional unit with its own characteristic reactivity.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: An ester should be recognized as one functional group whose reactivity is governed by the whole ester structure, not as two independent fragments.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should analyze the ester's overall functional-group behavior and apply ester-specific reactivity patterns when predicting mechanism steps.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the students frequently talked about the ester as if it were a carbonyl attached to an ether, rather than as a single unit that would have a characteristic reactivity."
misconceptions.prevalence: frequently
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students try to use vinyl group electrons to attack a cyclobutane ring and open it directly.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The correct pathway requires a preparatory electrocyclic ring opening before the Diels–Alder step; the vinyl electrons should not be used to directly break the unactivated C–C bond.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize when a reaction requires an initial reorganization step that generates the reactive intermediate needed for the next transformation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "12 of the 14 participants tried to do the same thing, using the vinyl group electrons to attack the four-membered ring."
misconceptions.prevalence: 12 of the 14 participants
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students ignore preparatory steps because those steps do not immediately generate product.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Some mechanisms require preparatory transformations before the key bond-forming step can occur.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should consider whether a seemingly indirect step is necessary to set up the next mechanistic event, even if it does not itself resemble the final product change.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Because they focused upon only those steps that would generate some aspect of the product, the participants were unlikely to take the necessary steps used to prepare for another, often key, step."
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students stop after deprotonation if they cannot immediately see that it leads to product formation.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Deprotonation can be a necessary preparatory step that enables a later mechanistic event, such as acting as a base in the subsequent step.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should ask what role the deprotonated species will play next rather than dismissing the step because it is not immediately productive.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Then I don't know, it's going to reprotonate or something. That's not, but that's not. What I'm saying is that's not getting me towards a product."
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think atoms in starting material and product are static and cannot move or be reoriented in space.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecules can be rotated, flipped, and conformationally reoriented when mapping starting materials to products; atom correspondences are not fixed by the drawing.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that structural drawings can represent the same molecule in different orientations and should map atoms based on connectivity and transformation, not on fixed page positions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I automatically labeled this oxygen 1 and oxygen 2 like they couldn't move. And that's silly."
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot determine the first intermediate or 'cue' for how to begin connecting arrows and therefore struggle to start the problem.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A mechanism should begin with a chemically justified first step based on substrate reactivity and reaction conditions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the initial reactive event from the structure and conditions, then build the mechanism from that first plausible intermediate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The students' inability to determine the first intermediate ... was one reason why participants often found it hard to even start a problem."
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students identify a reaction type first and then use arrows to force the mechanism to match that label.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reaction type should be inferred from the actual chemistry and then used to justify each step, not imposed mechanically on the substrate.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate the substrate and reagents to determine whether a proposed elimination, substitution, or cycloaddition is chemically appropriate before drawing arrows.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I knew I had to get rid of a hydrogen, through an elimination reaction to form this double bond."
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not correlate curved arrows with underlying chemical principles; they see bonds moving rather than electron flow and mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Curved arrows should be tied to fundamental chemical concepts such as nucleophilicity, basicity, proton transfer, and bond-making/bond-breaking events.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the concepts behind the arrows to explain why each electron movement is allowed and what driving force makes the step work.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "they need to correlate the curved arrows they draw with the fundamental principles of chemistry"
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can define Brønsted bases and nucleophiles but cannot distinguish them in applying them to mechanism problems.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Basicity and nucleophilicity are different concepts and must be applied appropriately depending on whether the step involves proton abstraction or attack on an electrophilic atom.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should decide whether a species is acting as a base or a nucleophile by examining the reaction context and the target of attack, not by memorized definitions alone.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "they could readily define the concepts of Brønsted bases and nucleophiles but were often hard pressed when asked to differentiate between the two while solving a problem"
misconceptions.prevalence: often; exact count not given
misconceptions.source_title: "It Gets Me to the Product": How Students Propose Organic Mechanisms

papers.paper_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Understandings of What Makes a Good Leaving Group

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a halide is a good leaving group simply because it is a halide.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Leaving group ability depends on the stability of the species after departure, especially whether the conjugate base is weak and stabilized by size, charge distribution, resonance/induction, and other structural factors.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate why the conjugate base is stable and weakly basic, then use structural/electronic factors to compare leaving groups rather than labeling a halide as good by name alone.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "because it's a halide. I just know that halides are very good leaving groups."
misconceptions.prevalence: Several students; described as a commonly offered explanation. The paper does not give an exact count for this misconception.
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Understandings of What Makes a Good Leaving Group

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think electronegativity is the primary or sole reason halides are good leaving groups.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electronegativity can matter in some comparisons, but for halides size is more important; fluoride is actually the worst leaving group among halides despite being most electronegative.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare halides by considering size first, recognizing that the larger halides better stabilize negative charge and form weaker C–X bonds; electronegativity alone is not sufficient across atoms of very different sizes.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students, however, argued that electronegativity was the primary consideration to explain why halides are good leaving groups"
misconceptions.prevalence: Nineteen students provided explanations showing this or related incomplete reasoning about halide leaving groups.
misconceptions.population: Organic Chemistry II students who discussed halide leaving groups
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Understandings of What Makes a Good Leaving Group

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe good leaving groups are good because they gain an octet when they leave, implying octet acquisition is the key stabilizing factor.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Halides already have an octet before leaving; leaving group ability is not explained by 'gaining an octet' but by how stable and weakly basic the leaving species is after bond cleavage.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should realize that halide ions already satisfy the octet rule and should instead reason about charge stabilization, size, and bond strength in the conjugate base and the C–X bond.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "they thought that a covalently bonded bromine atom was not as stable because it 'shared' electrons, rather than 'having all of the electrons to itself once it has left'"
misconceptions.prevalence: Discussed as a common explanation among students; the paper does not provide an exact count.
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Understandings of What Makes a Good Leaving Group

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think halides are good leaving groups because they acquire a full octet and become stable anions after departure, even though the halide already had an octet while bonded.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The departing halide already has an octet; the correct explanation is that the resulting anion is weakly basic and stabilized by size and other factors, not that octet completion occurs upon leaving.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should track electron counts before and after bond cleavage and recognize that the electronic stabilization comes from being a weak base with a stabilized negative charge, not from octet completion.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "if it gets one more electron to fill the second shell, it becomes more stable than if it had seven in that second valence shell when it was neutral."
misconceptions.prevalence: Multiple students; the paper identifies this as another commonly offered explanation.
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Understandings of What Makes a Good Leaving Group

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think water is a good leaving group simply because it is uncharged.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Water is a good leaving group because protonation converts hydroxide into neutral water, which is the conjugate base of a strong acid and is therefore a weak base and relatively stable after departure.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect protonation to formation of neutral water, then reason that the neutral product is the weak conjugate base of a strong acid and therefore can leave more readily.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "water, which can be a pretty good leaving group, because it's pretty stable itself because it's an uncharged species."
misconceptions.prevalence: Several students focused on this idea; no exact count is given.
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Understandings of What Makes a Good Leaving Group

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think water is a good leaving group because it gains an octet when it leaves.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Water leaving ability should be explained by the stability and weak basicity of the neutral leaving group after protonation, not by octet gain.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should see that water already has a filled valence shell and that the important issue is conversion of a poor leaving group (OH-) into a better one (H2O) by protonation.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "when it's protonated it becomes, it's easier to leave... it would not have enough electrons to fulfill an octet."
misconceptions.prevalence: Several students focused on this idea; no exact count is given.
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Understandings of What Makes a Good Leaving Group

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think leaving group ability is an absolute binary property: a species is simply 'good' or 'bad' rather than varying along a continuum.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Leaving group ability is relative; some leaving groups are extremely poor, some are very good, and their abilities depend on comparative stability and basicity.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare leaving groups against each other using relative factors such as conjugate-base strength, charge stabilization, and structure, not memorize fixed labels.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "They did not discuss the relative nature of leaving group ability, e.g., the continuum from extremely poor leaving groups (very strong bases) to very good leaving groups (very weak bases)."
misconceptions.prevalence: More than 30% of the students in the sample were limited to making assertions without explanation and expressed ideas in absolute terms.
misconceptions.population: Study participants (n=36), especially those making unsupported assertions about leaving groups
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Understandings of What Makes a Good Leaving Group

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that if they learned a species was a good or bad leaving group in class, that memorized label is sufficient and no explanation is needed.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should be able to justify leaving group ability using underlying chemical reasoning, not only recall taught labels.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should explain the chemical basis for the classification, such as weak basicity and stabilization of the departing group, rather than stopping at 'that's what we learned.'
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "It's just these certain things that you are taught and you don't really remember why they are the way they are."
misconceptions.prevalence: Ten students made assertions about leaving groups but were unable to provide any explanation.
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Understandings of What Makes a Good Leaving Group

papers.paper_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Use of Electrostatics to Explain Reactivity

misconceptions.subtopic: formal charge as the only criterion for reactivity
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that if a molecule has no formal charges, it will not react; formal charge presence/absence is taken as the direct determinant of reactivity.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reactivity depends on the distribution of electron density, nucleophilicity/electrophilicity, and electrostatic interactions; neutral molecules can still react if partial charges and polar bonds create a favorable reactive site.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine bond polarity, partial charges, electron-rich and electron-poor sites, and leaving group ability to decide whether a reaction is possible rather than requiring explicit formal charges.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "if you don't have any positive or negative charges, nothing's going to move... and if everything's already neutral, it has no reason to move and react."
misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students consistently invoked formal charges to determine chemical reactivity.
misconceptions.population: 17 first-semester organic chemistry students interviewed at a research-intensive university
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Use of Electrostatics to Explain Reactivity

misconceptions.subtopic: formal charge as a proxy for nucleophile strength
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that a nucleophile/reactant is strong enough to react only when it bears a formal charge, often linked to metal counterions; neutral nucleophiles are treated as too weak or not reactive.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nucleophilicity and reactivity are not determined solely by formal charge; neutral species can be nucleophilic if their electron density and bonding environment make them able to attack an electrophile.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate lone pairs, electron density, bond polarity, leaving groups, and the electrophile rather than equating nucleophile strength with the presence of a formal charge or metal association.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "NH2 isn't like a strong base in this case because it's not like with a metal."
misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students consistently invoked formal charges to determine chemical reactivity.
misconceptions.population: 17 first-semester organic chemistry students interviewed at a research-intensive university
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Use of Electrostatics to Explain Reactivity

misconceptions.subtopic: stability equated with no formal charges
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that a molecule without formal charges is automatically stable and therefore unreactive.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Molecular stability and reactivity depend on the full electrostatic and structural context, including partial charges, electronegativity, and the presence of electrophilic sites; neutral molecules may still react.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should not stop at charge neutrality; they should identify whether there are polar bonds, partial charges, leaving groups, or other features that create a reaction pathway.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it's stable on its own. There's nothing that can really attack"
misconceptions.prevalence: 5 students consistently invoked formal charges to determine chemical reactivity.
misconceptions.population: 17 first-semester organic chemistry students interviewed at a research-intensive university
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Use of Electrostatics to Explain Reactivity

misconceptions.subtopic: formal charge only on metalated species
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that nitrogen-containing nucleophiles are only reactive when bonded to a metal and carrying a negative formal charge; neutral nitrogen species are not viewed as reactive.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nitrogen-containing species can be reactive in their neutral form depending on lone pair availability, protonation state, and the electrophile; a metal counterion is not required for all nucleophilic reactions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should assess the availability of a lone pair and the electron density on nitrogen, then compare it with the electrophilic center, instead of requiring a metal-derived formal charge.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "NH2 isn't like a strong base in this case because it's not like with a metal."
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in the formal-charge approach; specific student example Bailey.
misconceptions.population: 17 first-semester organic chemistry students interviewed at a research-intensive university
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Use of Electrostatics to Explain Reactivity

misconceptions.subtopic: memorized reaction patterns instead of conceptual reasoning
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe reactivity is something to recall from class experience or memorized patterns rather than infer from chemical principles.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reaction likelihood should be reasoned from mechanistic principles such as nucleophile/electrophile interactions, bond polarity, leaving group ability, and partial charges.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use structural features and electrostatics to predict reactivity, then justify the reaction using mechanistic logic rather than saying it is familiar from prior examples.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "it's just something that I think that might happen... just from experience, just like doing and going to class"
misconceptions.prevalence: 4 students consistently invoked memorized heuristics when determining reactivity.
misconceptions.population: 17 first-semester organic chemistry students interviewed at a research-intensive university
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Use of Electrostatics to Explain Reactivity

misconceptions.subtopic: electronegativity directly causes dipole-dipole attraction without explicit partial-charge reasoning
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat electronegativity alone as the explanation for intermolecular attraction, often using it as a direct cause of dipole-dipole forces without articulating partial charges or dipoles clearly.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electronegativity differences create bond polarity and partial charges, which produce molecular dipoles; those dipoles are what underlie dipole-dipole intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect electronegativity differences to partial charge development and then to the attraction between opposite partial charges on neighboring molecules.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I think it's the electron density, like, cloud moving towards the more electronegative because it has, like, it takes more."
misconceptions.prevalence: Many students used electronegativity for intermolecular forces; specific example in Bailey's and others' explanations.
misconceptions.population: 17 first-semester organic chemistry students interviewed at a research-intensive university
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Use of Electrostatics to Explain Reactivity

misconceptions.subtopic: formal charges and partial charges treated as separate, non-transferable ideas
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the electrostatics used for intermolecular forces do not apply to reactivity; they separate formal-charge reasoning for reactivity from partial-charge reasoning for intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The same electrostatic principles underpin both intermolecular forces and reactivity; partial charges, formal charges, and electron density are related and can all inform where reactions occur.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should transfer the idea that opposite charges attract and electron density matters from intermolecular forces into reaction reasoning to locate nucleophilic and electrophilic sites.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students varied their approaches between the two contexts"
misconceptions.prevalence: Described as a major pattern; most students varied their approaches between contexts, while only 3 students used electrostatics consistently across both.
misconceptions.population: 17 first-semester organic chemistry students interviewed at a research-intensive university
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Use of Electrostatics to Explain Reactivity

misconceptions.subtopic: neutrality as the reason molecules cannot react
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that neutral molecules have no reason to move or react because they lack charges.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Neutral molecules can react when there is an electron-rich site and an electron-poor site; reactivity is driven by local partial charges and orbital/electrostatic complementarity, not by the mere absence of net charge.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine the distribution of electrons and partial charges within neutral molecules and identify reactive centers even when both molecules are overall neutral.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "If you don't have any positive or negative charges, nothing's going to move to become neutral. And if everything's already neutral, it has no reason to move and react."
misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in the change-in-approach group, especially Trenton early in the interview.
misconceptions.population: 17 first-semester organic chemistry students interviewed at a research-intensive university
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Use of Electrostatics to Explain Reactivity

misconceptions.subtopic: symmetry or spread-out electrons imply no reactivity
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students infer that symmetrical molecules or electron density spread across a molecule means the molecule will not react.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Symmetry can affect how charges are distributed, but it does not by itself determine whether a molecule is reactive; reactivity depends on the specific presence and accessibility of electrophilic and nucleophilic sites.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use symmetry only as one clue about charge distribution and then check for electrophilic centers, leaving groups, and partial charges rather than concluding nonreactivity from symmetry alone.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I don't think they would react [...] symmetrical [...] I'm seeing a lot of electron density [...] all of those electrons [are] more spread out."
misconceptions.prevalence: Two students who changed approaches discussed the nonpolar set this way.
misconceptions.population: 17 first-semester organic chemistry students interviewed at a research-intensive university
misconceptions.source_title: Organic Chemistry Students' Use of Electrostatics to Explain Reactivity

papers.paper_title: Priority and Selectivity Rules To Help Students Predict Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that if an intermediate is 'stable' it will be unreactive and therefore stop the reaction from proceeding.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reaction pathways are favored by energetically accessible intermediates and lower activation barriers, not by assuming a stable intermediate cannot continue reacting.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare energy barriers and recognize that an intermediate can be relatively low in energy yet still react further if the next step is accessible; stability does not mean inertness.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "many students get confused by the idea of a 'stable intermediate', thinking that if it is stable then it will somehow be unreactive, and therefore stop the reaction proceeding."
misconceptions.population: students in an introductory first-year organic chemistry course
misconceptions.source_title: Priority and Selectivity Rules To Help Students Predict Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students move the curly arrow directly to the positive charge on a heteroatom, treating it like a carbocation or protonated carbon.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A positively charged heteroatom already has an octet; the correct mechanism is usually stepwise, attacking an adjacent atom and then restoring the lone pair on the heteroatom.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use formal charge and octet reasoning: the heteroatom is electron-poor but not octet-deficient, so electrons are not pushed 'into' the positive charge directly; instead, they attack the adjacent electrophilic site and then flow back to the heteroatom.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Many students want to move the curly arrow directly to the positive charge (as with  $C^+$  and  $H^+$ )—indeed, this is a major mechanistic misconception among students."
misconceptions.source_title: Priority and Selectivity Rules To Help Students Predict Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.subtopic: nucleophiles vs bases attacking electrophilic sites
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a base should attack a positively charged carbon directly in electrophilic aromatic substitution, or that it can remove the hydrogen attached to the positively charged carbon to complete deprotonation.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In electrophilic aromatic substitution, the base removes the appropriate proton to restore aromaticity; it does not directly attack the cationic carbon or remove the proton in a way that merely reproduces the same 6-electron cation without progressing the mechanism.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish base behavior from nucleophile behavior and use mechanism progression: the base abstracts a proton that allows electrons to re-form the aromatic system, rather than attacking the positively charged carbon itself.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "A common mistake here is to attack C<sup>+</sup> directly with the base... A second common mistake is to remove the hydrogen attached to C+ ."
misconceptions.source_title: Priority and Selectivity Rules To Help Students Predict Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.subtopic: electronegativity as a predictor of electron donation
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume that more electronegative atoms are better electron donors / more reactive nucleophiles because they are associated with charge.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Less electronegative atoms are generally better electron pair donors and thus more reactive nucleophiles because they hold electron density less tightly and overlap orbitals more effectively.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that nucleophilicity depends on how readily a lone pair can be donated; higher electronegativity means stronger attraction to the electron pair and poorer donation, while lower electronegativity makes donation easier.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Students find this intuitively very surprising, as they associate electronegativity with charge and hence with reactivity. Indeed, this is a significant misconception in mechanistic chemistry."
misconceptions.source_title: Priority and Selectivity Rules To Help Students Predict Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.subtopic: steric effects on nucleophiles versus bases
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think bulky electron-rich species are equally good nucleophiles and bases, or do not distinguish steric effects on nucleophilic attack from proton abstraction.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bulky reagents are less effective nucleophiles because steric hindrance impedes approach to carbon, but they may still act as bases because proton abstraction is less sterically demanding.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the size of the reacting site: nucleophilic attack on carbon is kinetically hindered by bulk, whereas removal of a small proton is less affected, so bulky reagents preferentially behave as bases.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "In general, less bulky reagents will be better able to donate a pair of electrons at the start of a mechanism."
misconceptions.source_title: Priority and Selectivity Rules To Help Students Predict Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think amides are at least as reactive as esters, or do not recognize that amides are significantly less reactive toward nucleophilic attack.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Amides are less reactive than esters because the nitrogen lone pair donates by mesomeric effect into the carbonyl, decreasing the partial positive character of the carbonyl carbon.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should inspect resonance/mesomeric donation from nitrogen into the carbonyl and conclude that this lowers carbonyl electrophilicity relative to esters, making amides less reactive.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "electronegative atoms are better electron pair donors (i.e., an amide is significantly less reactive than an ester)."
misconceptions.source_title: Priority and Selectivity Rules To Help Students Predict Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may choose the wrong epoxide carbon to attack, not recognizing that the less substituted carbon is preferred under the basic conditions shown.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Under basic conditions, nucleophilic opening of an epoxide occurs preferentially at the less substituted carbon because steric and electronic effects both favor that site.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the two epoxide carbons and choose the less hindered, more accessible carbon for attack when the epoxide is opened under basic conditions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the steric and electronic effects reinforce one another and lead to attack at the less-substituted carbon."
misconceptions.source_title: Priority and Selectivity Rules To Help Students Predict Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students fail to prefer the pathway that forms the more stable carbocation intermediate, or do not use carbocation stability to predict regioselectivity.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When different carbocation intermediates are possible, the more stable carbocation is favored and determines the major product.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the possible carbocations, assess inductive/hyperconjugative stabilization, and choose the pathway leading to the energetically more accessible intermediate and product.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "there is a choice of primary or secondary carbocation intermediates... Electronic effects (in this case, +I/hyperconjugation) favor the secondary carbocation intermediate"
misconceptions.source_title: Priority and Selectivity Rules To Help Students Predict Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.subtopic: formal charges after bond formation or heteroatom deprotonation
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students forget to add or remove formal charges appropriately during curved-arrow mechanisms, especially after forming a bond from a neutral lone pair or after a heteroatom regains its lone pair.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chemical equations and mechanisms must conserve charge; formal charges need to be updated whenever electrons move or a bond forms/breaks.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should track electron pairs and valence counts stepwise, assigning a positive charge when a neutral donor forms a bond and removing positive charge when the heteroatom regains its lone pair.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students must ensure they balance charges. Most commonly, students forget to introduce a positive charge when using a neutral lone pair to form a bond"
misconceptions.source_title: Priority and Selectivity Rules To Help Students Predict Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.subtopic: attack on carbon vs hydrogen in ambiguous cases
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not distinguish when a nucleophile should attack carbon versus when a base should attack hydrogen.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nucleophiles attack carbon electrophiles, whereas bases remove protons; the reaction pathway depends on whether the reagent is acting as a nucleophile or a base.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the reagent role first and then apply the corresponding site preference: carbon attack for nucleophiles, proton abstraction for bases.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "if the attacking species is a nucleophile, it will attack the carbon, whereas if it is a base, it will attack the hydrogen."
misconceptions.source_title: Priority and Selectivity Rules To Help Students Predict Organic Reaction Mechanisms

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students assume that all substitution reactions proceed by SN2-style concerted attack and leaving-group loss, even when the substrate and conditions favor SN1.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Some reactions proceed by SN1 when leaving-group departure to form a stabilized carbocation is favored and the nucleophile is weak; the order of steps can differ from SN2.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate nucleophile strength and carbocation stability; if carbocation formation is energetically accessible, loss of leaving group can occur first, followed by nucleophilic attack.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the priority rules would predict a plausible mechanism and the correct product, but would always suggest an SN2 mechanism... rather than SN1"
misconceptions.source_title: Priority and Selectivity Rules To Help Students Predict Organic Reaction Mechanisms

papers.paper_title: The Role of Multiple Teaching Strategies in Promoting Active Learning in Organic Chemistry

misconceptions.target_misconception: The student expects the unrearranged substitution product 2-bromo-3,3-dimethylbutane instead of the rearranged product.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN1 reactions can proceed through a carbocation intermediate that may rearrange to form a more stable carbocation before nucleophilic attack, leading to the rearranged product 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first identify ionization to form a carbocation, then consider possible hydride or alkyl shifts that produce a more stable carbocation, and finally show bromide attack at the rearranged carbocation to give the observed product.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "2-bromo-2,3 dimethylbutane is the observed product, not 2-bromo-3,3 dimethylbutane, which is what I expected."
misconceptions.population: students in the organic chemistry course completing dialogue assignments
misconceptions.source_title: The Role of Multiple Teaching Strategies in Promoting Active Learning in Organic Chemistry

papers.paper_title: Investigating the impact of using web‑based discussion tools on students' conceptual understanding and 21st century skills development in organic chemistry education

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students struggle to identify 2,2,4-trimethylpentane as an isomer of octane and confuse constitutional isomers.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: 2,2,4-trimethylpentane is a constitutional isomer of octane because it has the same molecular formula as octane but a different arrangement of atoms.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare molecular formulas first; if they match, then check whether the atoms are connected differently. Different connectivity with the same formula means constitutional isomerism.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "One among common misconception identifed was structural isomerism. In this context, students may struggle to identify and diferentiate between constitutional isomers, such as 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (Q12) and other alkanes, causing confusion when tasked with classifying it as an isomer of octane."
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of using web‑based discussion tools on students' conceptual understanding and 21st century skills development in organic chemistry education

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students confuse addition and substitution reactions, and may classify the reaction of ethyne with bromine as substitution rather than addition.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Ethyne reacts with bromine by electrophilic addition, producing a dibromoalkene, not by substitution.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that unsaturated hydrocarbons like alkynes undergo addition at the multiple bond. Bromine adds across the triple bond, so the product and mechanism indicate addition, not substitution.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students may confuse substitution and addition reactions, leading to incorrect identifcation of the reaction type. In this regards, many students misinterpreted the reaction of alkynes with halogens."
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of using web‑based discussion tools on students' conceptual understanding and 21st century skills development in organic chemistry education

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think C2H2 + Br2 is a substitution reaction analogous to ethane bromination.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: C2H2 + Br2 is an addition reaction that forms CHBr=CHBr (a dibromoalkene).
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should note that ethyne is unsaturated, so bromine adds to the multiple bond. The expected product structure confirms addition across the triple bond rather than replacement of H atoms.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "In the case of the reaction between ethyne (C₂H₂) and bromine (Br₂), several students incorrectly identifed it as a substitution reaction rather than an electrophilic addition reaction."
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of using web‑based discussion tools on students' conceptual understanding and 21st century skills development in organic chemistry education

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students overgeneralize alkane reactions to alkynes, treating bromine addition to ethyne like substitution in ethane.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Alkynes undergo addition with bromine; alkanes undergo substitution under radical conditions.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish saturated from unsaturated hydrocarbons. The presence of a multiple bond in an alkyne means addition across that bond, whereas substitution is characteristic of alkanes under appropriate conditions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "This misconception likely stems from overgeneralization of alkane reactions."
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of using web‑based discussion tools on students' conceptual understanding and 21st century skills development in organic chemistry education

misconceptions.subtopic: Alkyl halides and alcoholic silver nitrate test
misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think all bromine-containing compounds give a white precipitate with alcoholic AgNO3.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Only alkyl halides that can react under the test conditions give the precipitate; aryl halides such as bromobenzene do not react because the C–Br bond in aromatic compounds is more stable.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify whether the compound is an alkyl halide or an aryl halide before predicting the test result. Bond type and reactivity determine whether AgBr precipitate forms.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Many students may incorrectly predict that all bromine containing compounds will give a white precipitate. However, bromobenzene (an aryl halide) does not react with alcoholic AgNO₃"
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of using web‑based discussion tools on students' conceptual understanding and 21st century skills development in organic chemistry education

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot distinguish SN1 from SN2 and may think methyl chloride reacts faster than tert-butyl chloride because it is less sterically hindered.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: tert-Butyl chloride reacts rapidly via SN1 because tertiary carbocation formation is favored; methyl chloride does not react faster in this context.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first determine which mechanism is plausible from substrate structure. For SN1, carbocation stability controls rate, so a tertiary substrate reacts faster than a methyl substrate. Steric hindrance is not the deciding factor for SN1 rate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students may struggle to diferentiate between SN1 and SN2 mechanisms (Q36), particularly when predicting the reaction rate of various alkyl halides."
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of using web‑based discussion tools on students' conceptual understanding and 21st century skills development in organic chemistry education

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think smaller or less sterically hindered halides react faster in SN1 because they are smaller.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN1 rate depends mainly on carbocation stability, so tertiary halides react faster than primary or methyl halides.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate the stability of the carbocation intermediate formed in the rate-determining step. More stable carbocations form more readily and increase the SN1 reaction rate.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students may mistakenly think that a smaller molecule like methyl chloride would react faster because it is less sterically hindered. This misconception arises from an incomplete understanding of carbocation stability"
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of using web‑based discussion tools on students' conceptual understanding and 21st century skills development in organic chemistry education

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students confuse the product of acetonitrile reduction with ethylamine or dimethylamine instead of methylamine.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: LiAlH4 reduces nitriles to primary amines; acetonitrile (CH3CN) gives methylamine (CH3NH2).
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should track the carbon skeleton during reduction and remember that the nitrile carbon remains part of the product as one carbon unit, yielding a primary amine with the same carbon count plus one from the nitrile carbon arrangement.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "When acetonitrile (CH₃CN) is reduced with LiAlH₄, it forms methylamine (CH₃NH₂) (Q37). However, students may confuse the product with ethylamine or dimethylamine"
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of using web‑based discussion tools on students' conceptual understanding and 21st century skills development in organic chemistry education

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students classify dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromobutane with strong base as SN1 or E1 instead of E2.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The reaction proceeds by E2 elimination, a one-step process in which the strong base removes a β-hydrogen while the leaving group departs.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use reaction conditions to identify the mechanism: a strong base with a secondary alkyl halide favors E2. They should look for concerted elimination rather than stepwise ionization.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students may incorrectly identify the mechanism as SN1 or E1, assuming that all elimination reactions follow these pathways. In reality, this reaction proceeds via the E2 mechanism"
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of using web‑based discussion tools on students' conceptual understanding and 21st century skills development in organic chemistry education

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not understand regioselective elimination in E2 and therefore cannot predict the major Saytzeff product.
misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: E2 elimination is regioselective, often favoring the more substituted alkene (Saytzeff product) when conditions permit.
misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare possible elimination products and apply regioselectivity rules to identify which alkene is more substituted and therefore the major product under typical E2 conditions.
misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students may not grasp the concept of regioselective elimination in the E2 mechanism, leading to errors when predicting the major product (i.e., Saytzef product formation)."
misconceptions.source_title: Investigating the impact of using web‑based discussion tools on students' conceptual understanding and 21st century skills development in organic chemistry education

papers.paper_title: Students' Strategies, Struggles, and Successes with Mechanism Problem Solving in Organic Chemistry: A Scoping Review of the Research Literature

misconceptions.target_misconception: Students use the EPF mainly to connect reactants and products or as an afterthought rather than as a tool for mechanistic reasoning.
