all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Locate the candidate stereocenters on the ring, evaluate whether each carbon has four distinct attachments in the molecular context, and then determine whether the molecule is overall chiral or meso from its symmetry elements.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I think this molecule has a chirality center because I see a plane of symmetry. Hence, I responded that it is chiral"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 14 out of 33
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Resolution of racemates with chiral acids/bases
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think no enantiomeric product forms, or they do not understand that resolving a racemate with a chiral reagent gives diastereomeric salts that can be separated by crystallization.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Resolution of a racemate with a chiral acid or base forms diastereomeric salts, which have different solubilities and can be separated by crystallization, followed by regeneration of the enantiomer with acid or base.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Recognize that reacting an enantiomeric mixture with a chiral resolving agent creates diastereomers; then separate them by differing physical properties such as crystallization and recover the pure enantiomer afterward.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "PSCTs responded to no enantiomer production. This assertion is a misconception, as the reaction will yield a combination of diastereomeric salts"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Not quantified as a single count in the narrative; described as a misconception in the response to the resolution question
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Nucleophilic substitution of 1-chloropropane with sodium hydroxide
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think substituting NaOH into a haloalkane requires adding water and/or that the reaction should produce a metal or an unclear non-alcohol product.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A hydroxide ion acts as the nucleophile and replaces the halide leaving group to form an alcohol and a halide ion.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify OH- as the nucleophile, Cl- as the leaving group, and predict substitution of Cl by OH to give propan-1-ol plus chloride ion; no water or metal product is formed in the substitution product itself.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “If I substitute the NaOH into this haloalkane to produce alcohol, I will have to add water H2O in this reaction” (PSCT20).
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 20 out of 33 PSCTs had misconceptions on question 1.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Synthesis of propane-1-thiol by nucleophilic substitution
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students misidentify the product/group introduced in a substitution synthesis and misconstrue the reaction pathway for making propane-1-thiol.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Propane-1-thiol can be synthesized by nucleophilic substitution of a leaving group in 1-bromopropane with HS- to introduce the -SH group.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Recognize that the thiol product comes from replacing bromide with HS- in an alkyl halide substrate, so the product should contain the -SH functional group, not an unrelated structure.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Question 2 pertains to the potential use of a substitution reaction within the context of synthesis ... PSCT8 gave the answers shown in Figure 8. Figure 8 illustrates that PSCT8 had a misconception.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 21 out of 33 PSCTs had misconceptions on question 2.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students misconstrue the SN2 mechanism and do not correctly understand the single-step backside attack/transition state description.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN2 occurs in one concerted step with backside attack, a transition state, and inversion of configuration at the reacting carbon.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Reason from the nucleophile approaching 180° away from the leaving group, simultaneous bond making/breaking, and inversion at the stereocenter.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “PSCTs were unsuccessful in assigning the configurations to both the substrate and the product.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 23 out of 33 PSCTs had misconceptions on question 3.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the leaving group departs before the nucleophile arrives in SN1, rather than understanding the stepwise carbocation mechanism and subsequent nucleophilic attack.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN1 proceeds in two steps: first ionization to a carbocation, then nucleophilic attack on the planar carbocation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Reason that the substrate ionizes first to form a carbocation; only after that does the nucleophile attack, giving the substitution product.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “I think in the reaction, the leaving group will depart before the nucleophile arrives at the scene and the substrate will then react with the nucleophile, I guess.” (PSCT16)
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 9 out of 33 PSCTs had misconceptions on question 6.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Chloride leaving group and product prediction
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the reaction between an organohalide and sodium chloride gives alcohol, but they misinterpret the reagent/product details and by-product nature.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In substitution with sodium hydroxide, hydroxide replaces the halide to form an alcohol; sodium chloride is not the reagent that produces alcohol in this context.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Match the nucleophile to the leaving group: OH- substitutes for halide to form the alcohol product and halide leaves as an ion.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the interaction between an organohalide and sodium chloride would result in the formation of alcohol.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: The paper reports a significant number, but no exact count in this sentence; question 1 had 20/33 misconceptions.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not understand the formation and/or strength of ethyl Grignard reagent and give inaccurate answers about its behavior as a base.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Alkyl halides react with magnesium in dry ether to form Grignard reagents (RMgX), which are very strong bases/nucleophiles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Recognize the organohalide–magnesium insertion step and infer that the resulting organomagnesium compound is highly basic and reactive toward acidic protons.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Question 5 remained unanswered by most participants... the limited number of participants who tried to address the question provided inaccurate answers, suggesting that they did not grasp the underlying concepts.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Most participants; no exact percentage given.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think chirality means a molecule forms the same image as its mirror image or treat chirality as a property of a single atom with four different groups rather than of the whole molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A chiral molecule is non-superimposable on its mirror image and lacks an internal plane of symmetry; chirality is a property of the entire molecule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Determine whether the whole structure and its mirror image can be superimposed; if not, the molecule is chiral.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “It is a forming the same image on the mirror as the original one is called to be chiral” (PSCT 16).
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 21 out of 33 PSCTs had misconceptions on question 2 in stereochemistry.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a molecule is chiral simply because it cannot be superimposed and/or because a chiral center bonds with other molecules in a chain, without analyzing the structure correctly.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chirality must be determined by the molecular structure, including whether there is a stereocenter and whether the molecule is superimposable on its mirror image.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Inspect the structure for a stereocenter and symmetry; do not rely on vague statements about superimposability or bonding to other molecules.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “The molecule is chiral because chiral molecules are molecules, which cannot be superimposed and the chiral center bonds with other molecules or compounds in their chain” (PSCT 12).
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 23 out of 33 PSCTs were unable to provide a satisfactory explanation on question 3.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot correctly rank substituents and then assign the R or S configuration; they may orient the structure incorrectly and use the wrong sense of rotation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Assign priorities using CIP rules, orient the lowest priority group away, and read clockwise as R and anticlockwise as S.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Rank substituents by atomic number, place the lowest-priority group away from the viewer, then trace 1→2→3 to determine R or S.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “Ranking the four substituents is my problem. If I have to place -H away from me, then the other substituents must be placed next to each other such that the direction of travel will be anticlockwise (left turn)” (PSCT 18).
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 9 participants showed a lack of understanding; 20 out of 33 had misconceptions on question 4.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot reliably determine which molecules are mirror images or identify stereochemical relationships, and resort to guessing.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images; diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Identify stereocenters, compare configurations/mirror relationships systematically, and then classify molecules as enantiomers or diastereomers based on that comparison.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “I could see that these three molecules have two stereocenters. However, I cannot really tell which one is a mirror image of the other... I had no option but to just guess the answer” (PSCT 9).
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 21 out of 33 PSCTs experienced conceptual difficulties on question 7.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think seeing a plane of symmetry means a molecule is chiral, or they fail to locate chirality centers correctly in the ring system.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A chirality center is typically a carbon bonded to four different groups; the presence or absence of a plane of symmetry helps determine chirality, and symmetric molecules may be achiral or meso despite stereocenters.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Check each relevant carbon for four different substituents and assess whether the whole molecule is superimposable on its mirror image; a plane of symmetry indicates achirality, not chirality.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “I think this molecule has a chirality center because I see a plane of symmetry. Hence, I responded that it is chiral” (PSCT 20).
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 14 out of 33 PSCTs showed lack of comprehension on question 8.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Resolution of racemates with chiral acids/bases
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the reaction of a racemate with a chiral resolving agent produces no enantiomeric/diastereomeric separation or that crystallization is not involved in the resolution process.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A racemic mixture can react with a chiral resolving agent to form diastereomeric salts, which can be separated by crystallization; the enantiomer can then be regenerated by acid/base treatment.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Recognize that interaction with a chiral acid/base converts enantiomers into diastereomeric salts with different solubilities, allowing separation and recovery of the pure enantiomer.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “PSCTs responded to no enantiomer production. This assertion is a misconception, as the reaction will yield a combination of diastereomeric salts, which may be effectively isolated by means of crystallization.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Not quantified exactly in the quoted sentence; the paper reports that many PSCTs had limited knowledge, while 10/33 and 21/33 showed understanding in questions 9 and 10 respectively.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Assessing conceptual difficulties experienced by pre-service chemistry teachers in organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think lowest energy corresponds to a molecule being easiest to break apart, more reactive, or more strained/less stable.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Lowest energy corresponds to the conformation with the most favorable arrangement, here the equatorial substituent placement that minimizes repulsive interactions and is more stable.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the steric interactions in each chair conformation, recognize that equatorial substituents reduce 1,3-diaxial repulsions, and infer that lower repulsion means lower energy and greater stability.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Lowest energy means easiest to break apart."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 2 of 19 students
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of organic chemistry topics among fourth year chemistry students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students choose the trans product because they judge it to be the most stable or best steric arrangement, rather than using the reaction mechanism to predict a stereospecific syn addition product.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A stereospecific syn addition gives the cis product, because both groups add to the same side of the ring according to the mechanism.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the reaction mechanism to track the face of addition and predict that syn addition produces substituents on the same side, independent of which product looks more stable.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I think it's going to be [trans] because I think it's the best distribution of the methyl groups"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 5 of 19 students chose trans; 7 of 19 chose correctly
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of organic chemistry topics among fourth year chemistry students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students evaluate the proposed products instead of the reaction mechanism when deciding which mechanism is correct.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Correct mechanism selection should be based on electron flow, bond making/breaking, and whether the proposed mechanism is chemically valid, not on whether a product looks stable or familiar.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should follow the curved arrows, check conservation of valence/octet rules, and determine whether the stepwise electron movement produces a feasible mechanism before judging any products.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Actually, I'm going to look at the products."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented in multiple students' responses; exact count not given
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of organic chemistry topics among fourth year chemistry students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the longest carbon chain or greater distance of the leaving group from a phenyl group makes the substrate more reactive in S_N1.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: S_N1 reactivity depends on formation of the most stable carbocation; greater substitution at the reaction center increases reactivity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the carbon bearing the leaving group, determine the carbocation that would form, and choose the substrate that forms the most stable carbocation, typically the most substituted one.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the longer the hydrocarbon chain the more reactive."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 5 respondents gave this reasoning; only 3 of 19 answered correctly
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of organic chemistry topics among fourth year chemistry students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the relative distance between substituents determines cyclohexane chair stability, rather than axial versus equatorial placement.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Chair stability is determined by whether substituents are axial or equatorial; equatorial placement is favored because it reduces steric interactions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify each substituent as axial or equatorial and compare the steric interactions, especially 1,3-diaxial repulsions, to decide which conformation is lower in energy.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "if the methyl groups are further apart, then they are lower in energy"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented in multiple students' responses; exact count not given
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of organic chemistry topics among fourth year chemistry students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students misapply axial and equatorial labels, using them incorrectly when describing substituent positions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Axial substituents point roughly perpendicular to the ring plane, while equatorial substituents project outward around the ring equator; stability depends on this correct identification.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should correctly identify the geometry of each substituent in the chair conformation and then use those labels to infer steric strain and stability.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I'll probably say [distracter with two axial groups] because it has methyl groups in the equatorial position, which would lead to 1,3 steric hindrance or something."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: At least 2 students (Emil and Clara) plus Francesca misapplied the terms
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of organic chemistry topics among fourth year chemistry students

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Mislabeling non-aromatic resonance-stabilized rings as aromatic
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students attribute aromaticity to non-aromatic six-membered rings with one double bond or use aromaticity as the explanation for resonance stabilization where aromaticity is not present.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Aromaticity requires a specific conjugated cyclic π-electron system; resonance stabilization in a non-aromatic ring should not be described as aromaticity.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should examine the ring structure for cyclic conjugation, planarity, and π-electron count; if these criteria are not met, the structure may have resonance stabilization but is not aromatic.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Aromaticity is key to stability"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented in multiple students' explanations; exact count not given
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of organic chemistry topics among fourth year chemistry students

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Using inorganic chemistry term 'ligand' for organic substituents
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students refer to organic substituents or functional groups as ligands.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In IUPAC naming and organic structure description, these groups are substituents or functional groups, not ligands unless discussing coordination chemistry.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the terminology appropriate to the chemical context: identify functional groups/substituents on an organic molecule and reserve 'ligand' for coordination compounds.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "what the number one ligand is"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented in multiple responses; exact count not given
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of organic chemistry topics among fourth year chemistry students

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Central atom with three bonds and one lone pair
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a center with three bonded atoms and one lone pair could be square planar, applying an inorganic coordination geometry to a main-group atom.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A main-group atom with three bonds and one lone pair has tetrahedral electron geometry and trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry, not square planar.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should count electron domains around the atom, assign the electron-domain geometry from VSEPR, and derive the molecular shape accordingly.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the electron pair should be tetrahedral, but it could be square planar"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented in at least 2 students' responses
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of organic chemistry topics among fourth year chemistry students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat the most stable species as the most reactive.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: For the questions here, greater stability generally means lower reactivity; in S_N1, the more stable carbocation-forming substrate is more reactive because the intermediate is stabilized.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between the stability of reactants/intermediates and the kinetics of reaction, then use the mechanism to decide which species reacts faster.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "there is evidence that the relationship between the relative energies and reactivity of molecules still remains unclear to some students, as some chose the most stable species as the most reactive."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Described as present among some students; exact count not given
all_misconceptions.source_title: Alternative conceptions of organic chemistry topics among fourth year chemistry students

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students can correctly predict the product of a nucleophilic substitution reaction without understanding how the product forms, and may treat the mechanism as unnecessary or beyond what they need to know.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A correct product prediction should be supported by understanding and drawing the full reaction mechanism, including electron movement and intermediates.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the reaction conditions to the reaction pathway, identify the nucleophile, leaving group, and mechanism type, then use curved arrows to show how bonds break and form to produce the product.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students could predict the products of organic reactions, but struggled to provide reaction mechanisms for those same reactions"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: In the traditional spring course, 90/111 (81%) answered the product question correctly, but only 7/28 who attempted the mechanism did so correctly; 75% did not attempt the mechanism.
all_misconceptions.population: Undergraduate non-science majors in the traditional spring organic chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Implementing POGIL in the lecture and the Science Writing Heuristic in the laboratory—student perceptions and performance in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may think that earning a perfect laboratory report score means they understand and can independently reproduce the reaction mechanism later on an exam.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Understanding a mechanism requires being able to reconstruct it and apply it in a new context, not just reproduce a completed mechanism in a lab report.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the lab experience to understand why each step in the mechanism occurs, so that the mechanism can later be drawn from knowledge of reactivity rather than memorization or copying.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "32 students out of 111 received a perfect score on their laboratory report, which included a full mechanism ... Yet when asked to complete this same mechanism two weeks later on an exam, only five of these thirty-two students tried and only two of them were successful."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 32/111 students received perfect lab reports; only 5/32 attempted the same mechanism on the exam and 2/5 were successful
all_misconceptions.population: Undergraduate organic chemistry students in the traditional spring course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Implementing POGIL in the lecture and the Science Writing Heuristic in the laboratory—student perceptions and performance in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students may believe that identifying the reaction outcome is enough, even when they cannot explain the pathway that leads to that outcome.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Correct chemistry performance includes being able to explain the transformation mechanism, not only the final product.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason from reactants and conditions to the mechanistic steps that justify the product, demonstrating causal understanding rather than recognition alone.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "even though students could recognize reaction conditions and write the correct product, they did not understand how the product is formed."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: During the traditional spring semester, 90/111 (81%) answered the product question correctly, but only 7/28 attempted mechanisms were correct
all_misconceptions.population: Undergraduate students in the traditional spring organic chemistry course
all_misconceptions.source_title: Implementing POGIL in the lecture and the Science Writing Heuristic in the laboratory—student perceptions and performance in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Chemistry problems should have one definite right answer, with all other answers being wrong.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Organic chemistry often allows multiple valid products, mechanisms, or synthetic pathways, and students must evaluate which is most appropriate for the context.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that the correct outcome depends on reagents, conditions, and the problem context; they should compare alternatives rather than assume a single absolute answer exists.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "there's right, there's right and wrong answers. There's not, like, \"how do you feel about this?\""
all_misconceptions.prevalence: At least 7 students described organic chemistry as 'straightforward'; multiple students expressed this view.
all_misconceptions.population: 18 organic chemistry students in a spiral curriculum; examples from Charlie and Luna
all_misconceptions.source_title: Perry's Scheme of Intellectual and Epistemological Development as a framework for describing student difficulties in learning organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: One starting compound treated with one set of reagents should lead to only one correct product.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Substitution and elimination reactions can produce more than one correct product, including mixtures, depending on conditions and mechanism.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should analyze the mechanism and reaction conditions to determine whether SN1/SN2/E1/E2 pathways compete and whether multiple products are plausible.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students found it difficult to accept that *one* starting compound treated with only *one* set of reagents could lead to more than one correct product"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Reported as a common difficulty among many students; no exact percentage given.
all_misconceptions.population: Organic chemistry students in the study, especially those discussing substitution/elimination reactions
all_misconceptions.source_title: Perry's Scheme of Intellectual and Epistemological Development as a framework for describing student difficulties in learning organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A reaction follows a simple one-to-one pattern such as A yields B, rather than potentially yielding multiple products such as A yields both B and C.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Some organic reactions can yield multiple products from the same starting material depending on competing pathways and reaction conditions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should consider competing mechanisms and evaluate all feasible products rather than expecting a single linear transformation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students who had expected organic chemistry to follow a pattern of 'A yields B and then B yields C' faced a problematic transition to 'A yields both B and C'."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Described as a major source of difficulty for many students; no exact percentage given.
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the organic chemistry sequence
all_misconceptions.source_title: Perry's Scheme of Intellectual and Epistemological Development as a framework for describing student difficulties in learning organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A synthesis problem should have one obvious route, so designing a synthesis is mainly a matter of remembering a single reaction rather than choosing among alternatives.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Synthesis problems often have multiple feasible routes, and students must judge which pathway or reagent set is best for the target compound and constraints.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should work backward or forward through several possible transformations, compare reagent sets, and select the most viable route based on selectivity, feasibility, and functional group compatibility.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Having to put everything together and sort of use your creativity, and knowing that I know everything solid to come up with a synthesis problem is difficult."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Reported by Marietta and echoed by Luna as a major obstacle; no exact percentage given.
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the spring semester of organic chemistry
all_misconceptions.source_title: Perry's Scheme of Intellectual and Epistemological Development as a framework for describing student difficulties in learning organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Knowing one reagent pair for a transformation is sufficient because the same reaction will always be the needed answer.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Different substrates and target transformations may require different reagents, and students need to know several possible methods for similar transformations.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the functional group being transformed with the specific reaction goal and compare alternative reagents rather than memorize only one example.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "you can remember just that one but if you need five options just in case it's one of the other options that's given on the test"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Common enough to be discussed as a general struggle in synthesis; no exact percentage given.
all_misconceptions.population: Students struggling with multi-step synthesis in organic chemistry
all_misconceptions.source_title: Perry's Scheme of Intellectual and Epistemological Development as a framework for describing student difficulties in learning organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: If several reaction pathways are available, all are equally acceptable and the task is just to produce any route.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: When multiple synthetic routes exist, students must evaluate which pathway is best or most viable for the target synthesis.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare pathways using criteria such as efficiency, selectivity, availability of reagents, and functional group compatibility to choose the best synthesis.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students were frequently required to judge, as emerging organic chemists, which set of reagents or pathway was 'best'."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Described as a frequent requirement; no exact percentage given.
all_misconceptions.population: Students in the organic chemistry sequence, especially during spring synthesis work
all_misconceptions.source_title: Perry's Scheme of Intellectual and Epistemological Development as a framework for describing student difficulties in learning organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Question 1a: choosing between substitution and elimination
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that if the starting material contains a double bond, the reaction should be substitution rather than elimination.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The presence of a double bond in the substrate does not determine whether substitution or elimination occurs; the mechanism is determined by reagent properties and reaction conditions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate the reagent as a base and/or nucleophile, its strength, the substrate, leaving group, and solvent to decide whether SN1, SN2, E1, or E2 is favored, rather than using the mere presence of a double bond as a cue.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the presence of a double bond in the starting material implies that a substitution is the reaction to be done."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that the presence of a solvent means substitution should be performed.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A solvent alone does not determine the mechanism; the full set of reactants and their chemical roles must be considered.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize that solvent identity is only one factor, and should analyze whether the reagent is acting as a base or nucleophile and whether the conditions favor SN1/E1 or SN2/E2.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the presence of a solvent in the starting materials implies that a substitution is the reaction to be done."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that a protic solvent automatically means substitution must occur.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A protic solvent can influence mechanism selection, but it does not by itself force substitution; the reagent strength and substrate also matter.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that protic solvents often favor carbocation pathways, but then still determine whether the reagent is a weak nucleophile/base or a strong nucleophile/base and which mechanism is actually favored.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the presence of a protic solvent implies that a substitution reaction must be performed."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that if methanol is present, substitution must be the reaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Methanol can function as both a weak nucleophile and a weak base, so it can support SN1 and E1 pathways rather than forcing substitution only.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should classify methanol by its chemical role and strength, then infer that weak nucleophiles and weak bases can participate in SN1/E1 outcomes depending on the substrate and conditions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the presence of CH3OH as a reagent always implies that a substitution reaction must be performed."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think SN1 only causes inversion of stereochemistry, like SN2.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN1 proceeds through a planar carbocation intermediate and therefore can give racemization rather than simple inversion.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the carbocation intermediate in SN1, recognize that nucleophilic attack can occur from either face, and infer formation of both enantiomers.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "$S_N1$, it attacks from the backside so it flips and it makes it go out."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a racemic mixture means one SN1 product and one E1 product.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A racemic mixture means two enantiomeric products from the same substitution pathway, not one substitution product plus one elimination product.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect racemization to attack on a planar carbocation intermediate and realize that both products arise from SN1 substitution.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "That one of them is an $S_N1$, and the other one is an E1."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think methanol behaves as an Arrhenius base that supplies hydroxide ions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Methanol is a covalent molecule and, in this context, acts as a weak base/nucleophile; it does not produce hydroxide ions as an Arrhenius base would.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish ionic hydroxide-containing bases from covalent alcohols and identify methanol as a neutral molecule that can accept a proton only weakly.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "CH3OH behaves as an Arrhenius base"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Question 1a: OH versus OCH3 in product
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that if the nucleophile contains an OH group, the product must substitute in the OH group rather than the methoxy group.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In methanol substitution, the oxygen-bearing methoxy group is incorporated; the product is not formed by simply adding hydroxide as if methanol were an ionic hydroxide source.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should track atom connectivity through the mechanism and recognize that methanol acts as CH3OH, not as free OH−, so the substituent introduced is OCH3 after proton transfer.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "if the nucleophile has an OH group, that one is necessarily the group that substitutes"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that if the starting material shows stereochemistry, the product must have inverted stereochemistry.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Whether inversion occurs depends on the mechanism; SN2 gives inversion, but SN1 does not necessarily do so.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should first determine the mechanism, then apply the correct stereochemical consequence of that mechanism rather than using stereochemistry in the starting material as a blanket cue.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "If a starting material shows stereochemistry, the product must have an inverted stereochemistry."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Question 1a: weak/strong base and substitution mechanism
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think weak bases proceed by SN2 and strong bases proceed by SN1.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Strong bases generally favor elimination, while weak bases are more associated with SN1/E1 conditions; SN2 is favored by strong nucleophiles that are weak bases.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish base strength from nucleophilicity and match reagent properties to the correct mechanism instead of reversing the relationships.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "weak bases proceed by $S_N$ 2 reactions and strong bases proceed by $S_N$ 1 reactions"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think SN2 conserves the stereochemistry of the starting material.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: SN2 proceeds by backside attack and gives inversion of configuration.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should recognize the concerted backside displacement in SN2 and predict inversion at the reacting stereocenter.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "$S_N2$ reactions conserve the stereochemistry of the starting material."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think elimination reactions are the only reactions that affect product stereochemistry.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Substitution reactions such as SN2 also affect stereochemistry, specifically by inversion.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect stereochemical outcomes to the specific mechanism, not assume only elimination changes stereochemistry.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Elimination reactions are the only ones that affect the stereochemistry of the product."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think an aprotic solvent means elimination will occur.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Aprotic solvents often favor SN2 reactions by supporting concerted mechanisms and not strongly solvating nucleophiles; they do not signal elimination by themselves.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use solvent type as one factor in deciding mechanism and should relate polar aprotic solvents to SN2 rather than elimination.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The presence of an aprotic solvent implies that an elimination reaction is to be performed."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a sodium cation can act as a nucleophile.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Sodium cation is not a nucleophile; the nucleophilic species is iodide from NaI.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify the negatively charged or electron-rich species as the nucleophile and recognize that Na+ is a spectator cation.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "A sodium cation can act as a nucleophile."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think E2 reactions have a carbocation intermediate.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: E2 is a concerted elimination with no carbocation intermediate.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should identify that the base removes a proton as the leaving group departs simultaneously, producing an alkene through a single transition state.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "E2 reactions have a carbocation intermediate"
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the hydrogen removed in elimination is the one on the carbon with the most hydrogens attached.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The proton removed in E2 is determined by anti-coplanar geometry and product stability, not by the simple count of hydrogens on a carbon.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate which beta hydrogen is anti-coplanar to the leaving group and which elimination pathway is mechanistically allowed and favorable.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "During an elimination reaction, the hydrogen atom is abstracted from the carbon atom that has the most hydrogen atoms bonded to it."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Question 1c: stereochemistry cue for alkene position
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that if stereochemistry is present in the alkyl halide, the least substituted alkene must be formed.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Stereochemistry in the substrate does not by itself determine that the least substituted alkene forms; E2 regiochemistry depends on the anti-coplanar arrangement and available beta hydrogens.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use E2 geometry and product stability, not the mere presence of stereochemistry in the substrate, to predict the alkene product.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The presence of stereochemistry in the alkyl halide implies that the least substituted alkene must be formed as a product."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think elimination must happen as far away as possible from the most substituted carbon atom.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The elimination site is determined by the allowed E2 geometry and the stability of the resulting alkene, not by a general rule of being far from the most substituted carbon.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should locate the anti-coplanar beta hydrogen and then determine which alkene is actually formed from the permitted E2 pathway.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the elimination reaction must happen as far away as possible from the most substituted carbon atom."
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Question 1c: most stable alkene always forms
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the most stable alkene will always be formed during elimination.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The most stable alkene is not always the product; the actual product depends on mechanism, steric constraints, and stereochemical requirements such as anti-coplanarity in E2.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should weigh alkene stability against mechanistic feasibility and choose the product permitted by the reaction pathway under the given conditions.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The most stable alkene will always be formed during an elimination reaction."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 6 participants
all_misconceptions.population: Sub-group 2a of question 1c (6 undergraduate organic chemistry students)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Question 1c: absence of double bond cue
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that if the alkyl halide does not already contain a double bond, elimination must be performed.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The presence or absence of a double bond in the starting material does not determine whether elimination occurs; elimination is determined by the reaction conditions and available beta hydrogens.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should analyze the reagent as a base and the substrate geometry rather than assuming elimination from the absence of a double bond.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "the absence of a double bond in the alkyl halide implies that an elimination reaction is to be performed."
all_misconceptions.population: Sub-group 2a of question 1c (6 undergraduate organic chemistry students)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think any structurally viable alkene can be formed in an elimination reaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Only alkenes consistent with the mechanism and stereochemical constraints of the reaction are possible; in this case E2 geometry restricts the product set.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should check which beta hydrogen is anti-coplanar and which alkene results from the allowed elimination pathway, rather than treating all possible alkenes as equally valid.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Any structurally viable alkene is possible when performing an elimination reaction."
all_misconceptions.population: Sub-group 2a of question 1c (6 undergraduate organic chemistry students)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Question 1c: charges on ionic reagent cue
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that explicitly showing separate charges in an ionic reagent means substitution must occur.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The charge depiction in a reagent does not by itself determine substitution; the reagent's chemical role and reaction conditions matter.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should interpret sodium methoxide as a base/nucleophile and then decide between E2 and substitution based on sterics and mechanism, not on charge notation alone.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The explicit depiction of separate charges in an ionic reagent implies that a substitution reaction must be performed."
all_misconceptions.population: Sub-group 2b of question 1c (10 undergraduate organic chemistry students)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think that if stereochemistry is shown in the alkyl halide, then SN2 must be performed.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Stereochemistry in the substrate does not automatically indicate SN2; the mechanism depends on base strength, steric hindrance, and other conditions.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should evaluate whether backside attack is feasible and whether the reagent favors substitution or elimination, rather than using stereochemical notation as a shortcut to SN2.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "The presence of stereochemistry in the alkyl halide implies that an $S_{\rm N}2$ reaction is to be performed."
all_misconceptions.population: Sub-group 2b of question 1c (10 undergraduate organic chemistry students)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think elimination reactions only happen with bulky bases.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Elimination can occur with both bulky and unhindered bases; base strength, sterics, and substrate control whether E2 is favored.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish between the role of base strength and steric hindrance and avoid restricting elimination to bulky bases only.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Elimination reactions only happen with bulky bases."
all_misconceptions.population: Sub-group 2b of question 1c (10 undergraduate organic chemistry students)
all_misconceptions.source_title: Students' understanding of alkyl halide reactions in undergraduate organic chemistry

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A nucleophile must be negatively charged, and an electrophile must be positively charged.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nucleophiles and electrophiles are defined by electron-pair donating or accepting behavior; charge can be a clue but is not required.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should determine whether a species can donate electron density to form a bond (nucleophile) or accept electron density into an empty/accepting orbital (electrophile), then use charge only as one possible indicator of that behavior.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Nucleophiles donate electron pairs, they're negative, and electrophiles, positive, they're the opposite."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 10 of 11 students mentioned charges in one or both definitions; 4 also considered partial charges.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Partial negative charge makes a species a nucleophile and partial positive charge makes a species an electrophile.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Partial charge can be one indicator of reactivity, but nucleophiles and electrophiles are identified by their ability to donate or accept electron pairs, not by charge alone.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should ask whether the species has electron density available for donation or an electron-deficient site/orbital available to accept electron density; partial charge may arise from structure but does not by itself define the species.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "they're electron dense, so they would have a minus charge, or partial minus, and then electrophiles are just the opposite... they would have partial positive or a completely positive charge."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 4 students considered partial charges in their definitions.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students focus on structural features such as charge or lone pairs instead of the actual electron-donating/electron-accepting function when defining nucleophiles and electrophiles.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A correct definition requires linking structure to function: a nucleophile donates electron density, and an electrophile accepts electron density.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect structural features (charge, lone pairs, empty orbitals) to what the species does in a reaction, rather than using structure as the definition itself.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students prioritize structure over function, relying primarily on charges to define and identify such species"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Described as the dominant pattern in the study; 10 of 11 mentioned charges.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Lone pair as essential feature of nucleophile
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: A nucleophile must have a lone pair of electrons.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A nucleophile is any electron-pair donor; lone pairs are common but not required because electrons in sigma or pi bonds can also act as nucleophiles.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify the species that can donate electron density in the reaction, which may be a lone pair, a bond, or another electron-rich region.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "A lone pair."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Barry distinguished this as his essential feature; the paper notes this idea was not fully correct because bond electrons can also be nucleophiles.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: An electrophile must have a positive charge.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: An electrophile is a species that accepts electron density; it may be positively charged, partially positive, or neutral if it has an electron-accepting orbital/site.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should look for electron deficiency and an available accepting site or orbital, not just an explicit positive charge.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I don't think it has to have a positive charge... I know positive charges are like usually a sign for them"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: At least 1 student (Barry) explicitly expressed uncertainty but still treated positive charge as the main sign; many others used positive charge similarly.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Smaller atoms or groups are more polarizable, and polarizability was confused with being a defining feature for nucleophiles/electrophiles.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Polarizability generally increases with larger, more diffuse electron clouds; it is relevant especially for nucleophilicity and does not mean smaller size.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should understand polarizability as the ease with which an electron cloud is distorted, which is greater for larger atoms or species with more diffuse electrons.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "one of them had, it helps if they're small and polarizable."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Only 2 students mentioned polarizability in their definitions.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Polarizability means electron density is pulled toward a more electronegative atom in a larger molecule.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Polarizability is the distortion of an electron cloud by an external force; it is distinct from bond polarization by induction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should distinguish between electron-cloud distortion in response to a perturbation and electron withdrawal caused by electronegativity differences in bonds.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "if there's a more electronegative atom, then the electron density will be pulled... towards that atom"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 1 student (Phoebe) explicitly showed this confusion.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Electrophiles are identified only by positive charge, without considering the need for an empty orbital or electron-accepting site.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: An electrophile must have an electron-deficient site capable of accepting electron density, often an empty orbital.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should connect electron deficiency to an available orbital/site that can accept a pair of electrons, not merely to charge status.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "they don't necessarily need to have a positive charge, they just need to... have, like an orbital that can be, um, like an empty orbital"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Only 1 student (Phoebe) articulated the correct orbital-based idea; most did not.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students must know or invent the reaction mechanism before they can identify whether a reaction involves a nucleophile and electrophile.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Whether a species is nucleophilic or electrophilic should be inferred from its electron-donating or electron-accepting behavior in the reaction, not from an already-drawn mechanism.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should examine the reactants and their reactivity directly; if they later use a mechanism, it should be checked for chemical feasibility rather than used as the sole basis for labels.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "students demonstrated that they needed to know the mechanism of a reaction before they were able to assess whether the reaction involved nucleophiles and electrophiles or not."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 71% of the 108 reaction evaluations involved students proposing mechanisms first (77/108).
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: If a student proposes a mechanism, whatever species is attacked in that proposed mechanism must be the electrophile, even if the mechanism is chemically impossible.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Nucleophile and electrophile labels must be based on actual reaction chemistry and feasible mechanism, not on a guessed or incorrect arrow-pushing scheme.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should test whether the proposed mechanism is chemically plausible; only then should they assign nucleophile/electrophile roles to real reacting species.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "their identification of the nucleophile and electrophile was based on that mechanism. Hence if the mechanism was incorrect, the students identified nonexistent intermediates as nucleophiles or electrophiles"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Documented repeatedly; e.g., 4 students proposed an S_N1 mechanism for reaction A and identified a nonexistent carbocation intermediate as electrophile.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Any negatively charged species is a nucleophile and any positively charged species is an electrophile, regardless of the reaction context.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Charge is only a clue; the species must actually function as an electron-pair donor or acceptor in the specific reaction.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should consider the full reaction context, including whether the species is acting as a base, acid, or something else, and whether electron donation/acceptance occurs.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "anytime there's a negative charge it's gonna be a nucleophile"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Repeated across multiple reactions; for reaction B, 8 students proposed ionic mechanisms and then assigned nucleophile/electrophile by charge.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Hydroxide is always a nucleophile, even in proton-transfer reactions where it is functioning as a Brønsted base.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A Brønsted base is identified by proton acceptance; a nucleophile is an electron-pair donor in bond-forming attack, and the two roles are not interchangeable.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should determine whether the reaction is a proton transfer or a nucleophilic attack, then assign roles accordingly; hydroxide may be a base rather than a nucleophile.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "I think this [hydroxide] is a nucleophile, pretty much sticking to that, um... just because I think I memorized it as a nucleophile."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Multiple instances; the paper notes 13 instances of identifying a nucleophile without an electrophile, several involving hydroxide in acid-base reactions.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: If a nucleophile attacks a proton in an acid-base reaction, the proton donor/carboxylic acid must be the electrophile of the reaction.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: In acid-base proton transfer, the reaction should be understood as Brønsted acid-base chemistry, not as a nucleophile-electrophile mechanism in the organic sense used in this study.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should first recognize proton transfer and the acid/base roles; labels of nucleophile/electrophile should not be forced onto every proton-transfer reaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "And I believe this [hydroxide] is a nucleophile. Which by default makes this [carboxylic acid] the electrophile of the reaction."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Observed in multiple students' responses to reaction E.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Treating carbonyl carbon as electrophile by default
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Any carbonyl carbon is automatically an electrophile, even in a carboxylic acid where the functional group behaves differently from an aldehyde or ketone.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Electrophilicity depends on the full functional group and reaction context; a carboxylic acid should be recognized as a proton donor in acid-base chemistry, not just as a generic carbonyl electrophile.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: Students should identify the whole functional group and its reactivity before assigning electrophile status, rather than focusing only on the carbonyl carbon’s partial positive charge.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "These students were so focused on recognizing the carbonyl group, that they failed to recognize that the carbonyl here is not a simple aldehyde or ketone, but rather part of a larger functional group with very different reactivity."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Several students misclassified reaction E when products were omitted.
all_misconceptions.source_title: Organic chemistry students' ideas about nucleophiles and electrophiles: the role of charges and mechanisms

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students do not correctly predict the product of a given alcohol substitution or elimination reaction, often confusing which product should form from the reagent and starting alcohol.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: The product depends on the alcohol structure and the reagent/reaction conditions; students should identify the correct substitution or elimination product from the reaction pathway.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should inspect the starting alcohol and reagent, determine whether the conditions favor substitution or elimination, then apply the corresponding reaction logic to predict the major product structure before drawing it.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students were asked to (1) predict the product of a given reaction
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Quiz mean product prediction score increased from 2.04 to 3.43 after gameplay.
all_misconceptions.population: 42 second-semester introductory undergraduate organic chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMCompete-II: An Organic Chemistry Card Game To Differentiate between Substitution and Elimination Reactions of Alcohols

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students struggle to classify alcohol reactions as substitution versus elimination, and to distinguish among SN1, SN2, E1, and E2 outcomes.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should classify a reaction by analyzing the alcohol type and reagent conditions to decide whether the reaction proceeds by substitution or elimination, and which specific mechanism is appropriate.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the substrate class and reagent type to infer the reaction pathway, then assign the correct reaction type based on the mechanistic conditions rather than guessing from surface features.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students were asked to (2) classify the reaction
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Quiz mean reaction classification score increased from 1.76 to 2.90 after gameplay.
all_misconceptions.population: 42 second-semester introductory undergraduate organic chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMCompete-II: An Organic Chemistry Card Game To Differentiate between Substitution and Elimination Reactions of Alcohols

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students cannot readily draw a reasonable mechanism for alcohol substitution or elimination reactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Students should draw a mechanistically reasonable sequence of electron-pushing steps that matches the identified substitution or elimination pathway.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect the classified reaction type to the mechanistic steps, then use curved arrows and intermediates consistent with the chosen SN1, SN2, E1, or E2 pathway to complete the mechanism.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: students were asked to (3) draw a reasonable mechanism
all_misconceptions.prevalence: Quiz mean mechanism score increased from 4.49 to 7.24 after gameplay.
all_misconceptions.population: 42 second-semester introductory undergraduate organic chemistry students
all_misconceptions.source_title: CHEMCompete-II: An Organic Chemistry Card Game To Differentiate between Substitution and Elimination Reactions of Alcohols

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students treat bond formation as requiring energy input, and use that to explain slower reactions.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond breaking requires energy input, whereas bond formation releases energy; reaction rate should not be justified by saying a reaction is slower because it requires energy to form a bond.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should distinguish endothermic bond breaking from exothermic bond formation and connect reaction rate to the overall energy profile and activation barrier, not to a blanket rule that bond formation needs energy.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the idea that Reaction A proceeds faster ‘because it requires less energy to form the bond’”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: mentioned as an unproductive resource in the analyzed student responses; no count given for this specific misconception
all_misconceptions.population: introductory organic chemistry laboratory students at the University of Michigan
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of organic chemistry students' developing reasoning elicited by a scaffolded case comparison activity

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a leaving group leaves because it ‘will require more energy to leave,’ treating leaving-group departure as something the molecule must energetically pay for without correctly linking this to bond breaking and the reaction coordinate.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: A leaving group departs when the reaction pathway and bond energetics make departure favorable; students should connect leaving-group ability to bond strength, stabilization of the departing group, and the activation barrier, rather than a vague idea that departure simply requires more energy.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should reason that weaker bonds and better stabilization of the leaving group lower the energy barrier for departure, which can facilitate a faster reaction.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “the methoxy leaving group ‘will require more energy to leave’”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: explicitly identified as part of developing energetics accounts; no separate count given for this misconception
all_misconceptions.population: introductory organic chemistry laboratory students at the University of Michigan
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of organic chemistry students' developing reasoning elicited by a scaffolded case comparison activity

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students use a simplistic rule that stronger bonds mean slower reactions because more energy is required to break them, without qualifying that bond strength must be considered within the mechanism and energy landscape.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Bond breaking requires energy, and weaker bonds are generally easier to break, but reaction rate depends on the overall mechanism and activation energy, not just a single blanket bond-strength rule.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should connect bond strength to the activation barrier and show how bond weakening can lower the energy needed to reach the transition state.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “The more energy required to break a bond, the slower the reaction.”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: found in the developing energetics account example; no percentage beyond the example provided
all_misconceptions.population: introductory organic chemistry laboratory students at the University of Michigan
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of organic chemistry students' developing reasoning elicited by a scaffolded case comparison activity

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Reaction speed vs. energy to form a bond
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think a reaction is faster if it requires less energy to form a new bond, implying bond formation energy is the key determinant of rate in these mechanisms.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Reaction rate should be explained through the activation energy of the rate-determining step and the overall energy profile, not by a simplified claim that less energy to form a bond automatically makes the reaction faster.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should relate the rate to the energy barrier to reach the transition state and identify which structural features reduce that barrier.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: “it requires less energy to form the bond to the oxygen of the alcohol group”
all_misconceptions.prevalence: embedded in the developing energetics account discussion; no count given
all_misconceptions.population: introductory organic chemistry laboratory students at the University of Michigan
all_misconceptions.source_title: Analysis of organic chemistry students' developing reasoning elicited by a scaffolded case comparison activity

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Leaving group size and leaving group ability
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that a larger halogen atom is automatically a better leaving group without necessarily connecting size to a deeper explanation.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Leaving group ability should be justified by how structural and electronic properties affect bond breaking and stabilization of the departing group, not by size alone.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should compare the halogens by asking whether a larger atomic radius leads to weaker C–X bonding and/or better stabilization of negative charge in the conjugate base, then relate those properties to easier departure.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "Bromine is larger than chlorine, and that would make [the bromine] a better leaving group"
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 4 students selected Reaction 2 activated size
all_misconceptions.population: Four second-semester organic chemistry students (Ivy, Shea, Ben, and Willam)
all_misconceptions.source_title: That's not a super important point: secondsemester organic chemistry students' lines of reasoning when comparing substitution reactions

all_misconceptions.subtopic: Leaving group size and periodic trend
all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students think the periodic trend in atomic radius by itself is sufficient to decide leaving group ability.
all_misconceptions.correct_answer_concept: Periodic trends are only useful when linked to bond strength and charge stabilization; size alone is not the endpoint of the explanation.
all_misconceptions.expected_reasoning: A student should use the fact that bromine is lower in the group to infer a larger radius, then explain how the larger atom better stabilizes the negative charge and weakens the C–Br bond, making leaving easier.
all_misconceptions.supporting_quote: "[The] atomic radius increases down the column. [The bromine] would be farther away from the carbon [and] easier to [...] leave."
all_misconceptions.prevalence: 3 of the 4 students who reasoned with size used an undeveloped line of reasoning
all_misconceptions.population: Second-semester organic chemistry students interviewed in the case-comparison task
all_misconceptions.source_title: That's not a super important point: secondsemester organic chemistry students' lines of reasoning when comparing substitution reactions

all_misconceptions.target_misconception: Students believe that if chlorine is more electronegative than bromine, chlorine is automatically the better leaving group, or that electronegativity alone decides leaving group ability.
